speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
Yesterday in this house, the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) raised a question of privilege about the report of the speech 1 made on Wednesday, May 22, which appears in Hansard beginning at page 151.
He explained to the house that a sentence had been deleted from my speech at my own request. I admit it is true, Mr. Speaker, and here is what happened.
An hour after we have made a speech, a blue copy of it is handed to us which we are asked to look over. As is the custom, I made a few style and vocabulary corrections which in no way altered the meaning of the text. And then I came up against a major difficulty. I felt an important sentence was missing. Since I was not allowed to add that sentence, I decided to delete a few words. I considered that, without that sentence, my text took on a wrong meaning or, at the very least, that the sentence had a significance other than the one I intended it to have. Therefore, I thank the hon. member for having given me this opportunity of making that correction to my text and four others which I also consider important.
On page 4 of the appendix, the words:
-as in Ontario.
should be added to the following sentence:
-while there is only 27 per cent of the labour force and twice as many unemployed people-
And to comply with the request of the hon. member, on page 5, after the sentence beginning as follows:
For instance, on the trains-
And ending with:
-and the stations are called only in English.
the following sentence should be inserted:
And while this is going on in Ottawa and on the trains, bombs are exploding in Montreal.
Finally, at the bottom of the second column of page 5, instead of:
-while paying, at the same time, the federal contribution-
One should read:
-while having the province assume, at the same time, the federal contribution of $75 million to hospital insurance-
1 trust, Mr. Speaker, that with leave of the house, those corrections will be made in the final version of Hansard. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that I apologize if I have unintentionally violated the rules of this house.

In the economic field, where do we stand? We own almost nothing.

Question of Privilege
As a motion taken at the time for matters of privilege is thereby given precedence over the prearranged program of public business, the Speaker requires to be satisfied, both that there is a prima facie case that a breach of privilege has been committed, and also that the matter is being raised at the earliest opportunity.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, May 27, consideration of the motion of Miss Pauline Jewitt for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to the speech from the throne delivered by His Excellency the Administrator at the opening of the session.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night at ten o'clock we were discussing some of the problems that face this country and the paucity of solutions in the speech from the throne. At the outset this morning I should like to re-emphasize my warning to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) that we in western Canada are going to be watching him very closely indeed.
I want to turn to the problems of confederation and some of the things that will have to be considered in order to make it really work. I think the first comment one should make is that some of the problems which we have to meet are problems resulting from the old Liberal policy of divide and rule. We are now suffering because of what happened during 20 years of Liberal rule, when they deliberately divided this country. I am hoping they will not do this again, but it is obvious that they are on the same track. We in western Canada are certainly concerned over this fact. As I said last evening, we are firm proponents of confederation. We want to see a whole Canada. We want to see a united Canada. In addition to that, we want to see a Canada run by Canadians without this interference from our neighbours in financial and political matters.
I believe that one of the prime responsibilities of the press in Canada is to take a new look at what they have been doing. I believe that on their doorstep lies the responsibility for some of this division which now exists in Canada. I suggest to some members of the press that they pay more attention to reporting the facts than to building up their own egos or images as Hollywood stars or as interpreters of the news. Most of them do not have the necessary background information to make an accurate interpretation of the news as they continually purport to do. They have a responsibility if they are going to maintain the freedom of the press in Canada, if they are going to do their part in promoting unity within Canada. This unity is necessary in order to make Canada a growing, developing country. If this unity is to be achieved, then the press must become more constructive, more positive in their approach

instead of continuing this negative, destructive approach which we have seen exhibited by some members of the press gallery and the press generally throughout Canada during the last two years.
I believe confederation can only work in Canada if all of us have as our goal a united Canada. The members of the press, having the prime responsibility for communication among the various ethnic groups, among the various regions in Canada, have not met their responsibilities. I am suggesting to them that they should pull up their socks and help us build Canada instead of destroying it.
I should like also to say something with regard to our position in the world. During the last election campaign we heard a lot of nonsense, some of it engendered by our friends in the press and all of it started by the Liberal party, to the effect that Canada's prestige abroad had gone down. This is such utter nonsense that it needs to be commented upon. I suggest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) that if Canada's prestige does not go down now that we have become a satellite of the United States in connection with nuclear arms, I will be very surprised. One of the things that struck us when we attended the commonwealth conference last fall was the fact that Canada could play a role with these newly developing countries in Africa and Asia. I will always remember the suggestion given to me by the Malayan delegate. He said "You people really are not part of the commonwealth at all; you are an appendage of the United States". If they thought of us in that fashion then, what must they be thinking of us now?
The Liberals talked about loss of prestige. Our prestige was never higher than under the leadership of the former prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker). Is it loss of prestige if a few newspaper reporters in certain countries such as the United States and the United Kingdom felt we were not doing exactly what they thought we should do? What utter nonsense. What utter irresponsibility by these people. I suggest that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will have to walk with his head bowed when he does return to the United Nations, because Canada will not be able to stand up and take the position she did previously. This situation will result from the decision, which is not final yet as far as I am concerned, regarding nuclear arms and our position in NOEAD.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to reemphasize the importance to Canada of making confederation work, the importance of taking these two languages and two nations and building them into one. Then there is the question of the division between urban and 28902-5-24
The Address-Mr. Olson rural people, which has been fostered by the daily press in Canada. I suggest that the members of the daily press should have a look at some of the things the weekly editors across this country have been saying, and should accept some advice from these people. We need better support from the members of the press if we are going to have a united Canada and a confederation that really works.

maintopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As I rise to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the many others who have extended to you and the Deputy Speaker, as well as the deputy chairman of committees, their sincere congratulations. If the manner in which the proceedings of this house have been handled so far is any indication of what we can expect in the future, I think all hon. members will be satisfied. I should like also to offer my sincere congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I do not wish to cover a lot of the ground that has been covered by hon. members who preceded me in this debate. In so far as the speech from the throne is concerned, first of all I should like to suggest that the preamble certainly does recognize the bicultural character of Canada. There are, however, one or two commonly held thoughts which I believe are erroneous which are brought out in the speech from the throne. The first is the separation of Quebec from the rest of Canada. There is a reference to the French sector, and the other nine provinces seem to be referred to as the English sector.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the past there existed the same division between eastern and western Canada. At that time the dividing line was somewhere west of lake Superior. We had repetitious references to the fact that there was a division along that line. I feel it would be unfortunate indeed if we were to now continue that line of thinking by moving the border to the Ottawa river. We have French communities in Alberta. We have French communities in many other parts of western Canada. In addition we have large numbers of people, even in my own riding, with French ancestry. I suggest too, Mr. Speaker, that we in western Canada have just as much in common with Montreal as we have with Toronto. For example in the clothing and needle trades I think it is fair to say western Canada buys more of this type of merchandise in Montreal than it does in Toronto. That is to say it buys more from Quebec than it does from Ontario. I shall not labour the matter at length except to point out I would not like to see a division
358	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Olson along the lines of separating Quebec from the rest of Canada in the so-called bicultural nature of our country.
People come from Quebec to western Canada just as young people in particular go to eastern Canada from Alberta, and there are social adjustments that have to be made in each case. I can remember that not so long ago three young fellows from the province of Quebec called at my farm. They had just enough English so that we could get along and communicate with each other, although certainly they were not too proficient in this language. It happened to be a season of the year when we required some additional help so we hired all three of them. That was several years ago. One of the young men proved capable and interested in the work and type of opportunity available there, and by now he has made a huge success of it. He adapted himself to the working conditions in the agricultural sector and now holds one of the best jobs in the area.
I have not followed the progress of the second young lad, but the third one could not adjust and I understand he went back to Quebec rather sadly disillusioned, if I may put it that way, with his experience in western Canada. By the same token young people from western Canada have moved to Toronto and Montreal, drawn by the bright lights and the opportunities they thought were just waiting for them. However, they were strangers in the large cities, and some of them have come back to western Canada pretty disillusioned with what they had thought were greener pastures.
I shall not say more about that at this time, except to state that I do not believe all the problems, in either English or French Canada, are going to be solved by bilingualism. People will learn other languages only when there is an economic need for them to do so. These language differences are not confined solely to Canada. Just a couple of days ago I noticed in the press where 1,500 people were demonstrating in Belgium with a view to separating Belgium into two countries, one for those who speak French and the other for those who speak Flemish. Language difficulties are also present in many other major countries. India and China have a multiplicity of languages which divide them and make communication among their peoples almost impossible.
Even in such a very small country as Nigeria, which we visited last fall, we found three separate languages, three large language groups, besides English. The western region, the eastern region and the northern region each had its own language, and people who


did not have the opportunity to learn the three languages simply could not communicate with one another except by the common language only a few of them had, and that was English. Therefore I do not appreciate the allegation that removing this language barrier in itself will solve the problem. Furthermore I do not believe there will be a determined effort, by those people who only have one or other of these languages, to learn a second language until there is an economic need for them to do so.
Mr. Speaker, the matter of Canada's commitments in international defence and her contribution to the western alliance has received a great deal of attention in this debate. I am happy to see that the government is proposing a resolution to set up a committee of 18 to study this problem. That committee will provide information, perhaps even classified or secret information, to members of all parties so we can have a fairly good idea what Canada's commitments are, and perhaps we can have unanimity as to what she should do to meet those commitments.
The other day I asked the Prime Minister whether he had taken any steps to renegotiate our commitments to the western alliance. His answer was not particularly clear, but I certainly did not ask the question with a view to embarrassing him or reminding him of one of his statements that he perhaps regretted having made; because I think there is some merit in his suggestion that we first of all meet the commitments we have made and then possibly renegotiate them so that we can take on a role more in keeping with Canada's position as a middle power in the world.
The reason I say this is that one of the greatest dangers in the world today is when we have a direct confrontation between the two major powers. The Secretary of State for External Affairs yesterday referred to this briefly, and looking back over the last two or three years I am sure we all agree that the periods of greatest tension were those two occasions when there was direct confrontation between the two major powers.
September, 1961 at Berlin, when Russian and United States tanks were facing each other across the border, was one of those occasions. My own feelings, and those of the community in which I live, were very tense in that situation. Quite frankly, I believe it would have been immeasurably safer had the troops on both sides of that border been troops from middle power nations. This would give the major powers an opportunity to sit back and perhaps referee the situation and allow it to cool off in case someone had accidentally

fired or misinterpreted a command, or something of that nature. Even today I shudder to think what would have happened in that situation had either United States or Russian troops opened fire.
Of course the greatest tension in recent history was when the confrontation of Americans and Russians took place on the high seas off Cuba. I am not suggesting there was a place in that situation where the middle nations could have avoided such a confrontation; nevertheless we can all agree that if there is a place and a role for the middle nations it is in such matters, so that we can keep the major powers from getting into a situation where either one or the other would lose face by backing down a little.
There are a number of other suggestions in the speech from the throne that could be very, very useful if properly implemented. The municipal development fund that is suggested is one of the most far reaching and useful proposals, if it is set up properly and if it becomes active enough to meet the demands that will be made on it. Of course we in this party over the years, and particularly during the last election campaign, suggested that the social capital or social credit necessary for the municipalities to meet their expansion requirements could be supplied far better from a branch of the Bank of Canada, rather than having them go out into the private money market where they must compete, with private industry, thus forcing up interest rates.
So we will have to wait until we have a more specific outline of what this measure is going to do. Certainly if it is set up properly I think it will be very, very useful. We have in Alberta a model, perhaps, that could be used in this regard. Although of course we do not have the resources of the Bank of Canada behind the municipal finance corporation out there, it certainly does give an opportunity for all municipalities in all parts of the province to obtain their social capital requirements at a rate of interest substantially lower than would be obtainable if each of them were to go to the money market individually to get these funds.
Therefore we will leave that for the moment, Mr. Speaker. I think our party will have a great deal to say in the debate that will take place on the setting up of this fund, because we look upon it as something that can be useful. On the other hand, we would not like to see it suffer the same fate as the municipal assistance program that was set up prior to 1940, which program simply disappeared.
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two other suggestions contained in the speech from the throne about which I have something to say.

The Address-Mr. Olson There is the proposal for a new department of agriculture act to be placed before parliament with a view to the appointment of a second minister of agriculture. I am a little apprehensive about this. I agree that the problems facing agriculture in eastern Canada are somewhat different than those in western Canada, but only in some aspects. I say this because certain agricultural products are common to both areas. It is just possible that this proposal, if carried out, will cause too much of a division in this department. To my mind this may create more problems than it would solve. On the other hand the proposal that there be an associate minister of agriculture who will give special attention to the problems of farmers in one particular area sounds a very good idea. We know this is a very large department and perhaps special attention should be given to certain areas.
I should like for a few moments, Mr. Speaker, to return to my own constituency. I would inform the house that the greatest problem there today is drought. This is a recurring problem that has been with us in a very severe way for the last four years. I am certainly not going to try to attach any blame for this to either the previous Conservative government or the present Liberal government. However, I want hon. members to know that while some of them speak of the hardships that come with an average income of $1,800 or $1,300, or various other figures, for the farming sectors of their constituencies, for the last four years in my constituency hundreds of farmers have had no income at all because of drought. In fact they have had substantial losses. They are now living on an accumulation of capital, not cash capital but depreciation and other things. Certainly this cannot go on very much longer.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to attach any blame to anyone for this, but I do hope some assistance will be provided by this government which will enable those who are vexed with this problem to get over this very trying period. Certainly when we look back over the weather patterns in this area we are convinced that this is going to change. In spite of the fact that the last drought period was longer and more severe than any in recorded weather history, we still hope that it will change. We hope it will change even this year. But if it does not, it will be necessary for both the provincial and federal governments to come forward with some assistance to at least maintain the breeding stock of the cattle business, and so

The Address-Mr. Olson on, so they will not be completely dissipated when the weather and drought conditions do improve.
One other serious problem in my constituency is the continual decrease in the output of the flour milling industry. Looking back over the records of our exports of flour we find that year after year for the last five or six years there have been decreases in the amount of flour Canada has exported, particularly to some of the nations in the Far East. I think it is fair and safe to say that the flour milling industry in Medicine Hat was established with a view to supplying the flour requirements of the Orient and some of the south Pacific countries. Some of these countries have of course established their own flour milling plants, in the last few years, and this is one of the main reasons for the decline in exports.
However, in Canada we produce in abundance the raw material that goes into this industry. I would urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture, when they go into the international markets to sell wheat or other food from Canada's surpluses, to take into consideration the fact that we already have a large, established flour milling industry which produces the highest quality flour. Perhaps in some of the wheat deals we are making part of the content could be made up of the finished product.
The matter of ARDA has been raised a number of times in this debate, and I want to say a word or two on this question. In the southeast corner of Alberta we have set up what is known as the short grass ARDA advisory committee. This committee is composed of a large number of organizations. I believe on the committee there are very competent men representing those organizations, and they have come forward with some very useful, practical and feasible suggestions to make use of what was anticipated in this act. No. 1 on their list of recommendations is the need for more positive information relating to ground water reserves for the southeast corner of Alberta. Many livestock operations are at the moment experiencing the most severe shortage of stock watering facilities in their history. This, of course, is because of the prolonged drought, but it is quite obvious that the most complete system of dams and dugouts is quite inadequate when there is no run-off to fill them. This committee says the immediate answer would appear to be water wells, but farmers are reluctant to dig wells after expensive failures with either dry holes or inadequate supplies of surface ground water.
The need is more widespread than just stock watering, as many small towns, villages and

hamlets are at the present time very short of good drinking water. They recommend- and I think it is a good recommendation- that a systematic ground water survey be undertaken to indicate large aquifers, underground channels or rivers and even supplies of water large enough to permit pump irrigation. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the ground water division of the Alberta research council has indicated what might be accomplished by its limited operations in this area. This committee also recommends that some additional encouragement and perhaps some financial assistance by way of long term credit be extended for the carrying out of proper and adequate land levelling in the irrigated areas of this part of Canada. I think it is generally agreed by all those who have studied the problems of the irrigated farm that many of the difficulties could be removed if there were adequate land levelling so the best possible use could be made of the acres "under the ditch".
One project which I think it would be appropriate to reassess at this time is the Redcliff-Ronalane irrigation scheme. There is new interest in the potentiality of some specialty crops and, moreover, there is the growing importance of livestock production in the constituency. The reason it is appropriate to reassess this project is because of the severe loss of stock water in the area resulting from the condition of extreme drought which has persisted during the last four years.
These are the suggestions I have to make regarding what could be done to assist as many farmers as possible in this area. I hope the Department of Agriculture or whoever is responsible for the ARDA program will give consideration to the proposals I have made.
There is one other point I have to make, and it concerns the establishment of a veterinary college in Alberta. I wish to urge the Minister of Agriculture in the most sincere way I know to make some financial contribution to this project at an early date. The province of Alberta is prepared to make a large contribution to set up this college in Edmonton, and to get it under way as soon as possible. I hope there will be no undue delay in doing so. It is interesting to note that a few days ago the Globe and Mail carried a story which read as follows:
There is a shortage of veterinarians throughout the world but the need is most acute in the developing countries, says the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization.
We have a shortage of veterinarians even in Canada, and we know that the facilities for training them are simply not adequate to meet the needs of our own people. This, I think, is an important consideration. Our exports of livestock to the United States may

at some stage reach a point where they will depend upon the manner in which we can control disease. So we are dependant upon having sufficient veterinarians to keep livestock diseases in check.
The Prime Minister said at the outset of this debate that he hoped some years from now we could all look back with pride on the work of the twenty sixth parliament. I hope this statement comes true. I also hope that when we do look back upon the first session of the twenty sixth parliament we will be able to say we achieved something for the good of Canada generally. In conclusion, may I say there are many details of the proposals set out in the speech from the throne which will be examined as each of these measures is brought to the floor of the House of Commons. I hope the legislation will be brought down as quickly as possible so that we may get on with our work and implement some of them for the well being of the people we represent.

speechtext:
My opening remarks will be characterized by sincerity if not by originality, Mr. Speaker. I should like to congratulate you warmly on your election and appointment as Speaker of this house.
The leader of the New Democratic party has already made it clear in this chamber that the members of this group are ready to give the government a chance to carry out the program outlined in the speech from the throne. To this end we offer hon. members opposite a high measure of co-operation- critical co-operation, but very real co-operation none the less. We shall seek to join with the government and with other parties in this house to make the twenty sixth parliament of Canada an effective instrument for the welfare of the people of Canada.
Perhaps, however, I should give a warning to those members of the government and their supporters who happen to be in the house. We do not suggest, by this offer of co-operation, that the millenium has arrived. We do not believe that politics are entirely banished from this house. Indeed, if the government does anything good we shall take the credit for it; if the government does anything bad, we shall point it out as clearly as we know how. I must say that the lamb- I think hon. members know to whom I refer -is not yet ready to lie down with the lion. We do not relish the thought of being inside that animal.
Seriously speaking, there are some goals of achievement which I believe this parliament should set before it. I know this is repetitive, but I believe, as the speech from the throne indicated, that the first and most urgent task which faces us is to conquer unemployment.
The Address-Mr. Brewin
No modern country can tolerate unemployment on the scale that has become chronic in Canada. The economic waste is obvious and staggering; the human waste is worse. There can be few members of this house who have not had the painful duty of telling numbers of their constituents, eager and anxious to find work, that there is nothing they can do to help immediately. This is particularly tragic when those who seek work are over 40 and are told that by reason of their age there is no place for them in the economic system. If someone were to come into this house and tell each member who is over 40 that he was to be retired for good, there would indeed be wailing and gnashing of teeth; and rightly so, because not many members would be left. There would be only a corporal's guard. Yet this is the experience which happens to hundreds of thousands of our constituents every day, and we must do something about it.
The speech from the throne contains promise of certain economic measures designed to deal with this overriding problem of unemployment. I hope these instruments will be used vigorously and fearlessly for the purpose of the economic planning that is essential. We must not only will the end of unemployment, we must also will the means necessary to end it. These means must include, as up to date economists concede, the large scale infusion of social capital into the economic system. In this connection, in my opinion, the provision of adequate housing has an important part to play.
I trust that the proposed municipal development and loan board will ensure that the projects to be financed include large scale plans for urban renewal, low rental public housing and rehabilitation of existing housing that is threatened with decay. In the metropolitan area of Toronto we are justly proud of the Regent Park development. A three bedroom apartment in Regent Park rents for $50.50 a month. A comparable apartment outside rents for $150 a month. In metropolitan Toronto it is estimated that at least 30,000 people are without a decent place to live. They are members of low income families who cannot afford proper housing. We need more and more Regent Park developments in this country.
It is often said that one of the major problems facing us is the high cost of living. In this problem the rental payments for those who rent, or the mortgage payments for those who have bought their own homes, is a major factor. We worry, and properly so, about small increases in the price of milk or bread or some such other essential commodity; I hear one of my colleagues mention sugar. The greatest pressure on the cost

The Address-Mr. Brewin of living today comes from the extremely high cost of another basic commodity, housing.
In my constituency the major problem of housing is the danger of the gradual depreciation and decay of the existing stock of housing, most of which was built some 50 or 60 years ago. Any housing program should include a plan for encouraging and giving incentive to bringing this existing stock of housing up to date; it should include incentives to improve facilities and the environment of areas which are already built up. The present housing act has done something to provide housing for medium income groups in suburbs, but it has done very little to rehabilitate and renew the existing stock of housing where you already have services, schools, and other things provided in the larger cities. The urban centre requires attention.
Mr. Speaker, I was glad to note that the speech from the throne made reference to amendments to the National Housing Act. These amendments, however useful, will not be enough. More is required. We need vigorous and active leadership from the federal government if we are really to tackle this problem of housing. There are already provisions in the National Housing Act for low rental housing. Again referring to metropolitan Toronto, they adopted a modest program for building 5,000 low rental units in five years. So far in the period they have produced only 550 units. I myself was connected indirectly with a project of the federal government in 1953 which was a partnership project with the government of Ontario under the National Housing Act. They acquired 1,800 acres of high class farming land in the neighbourhood of Toronto. They expropriated the farmers' property and turned them off their farms. It cost them nearly $2 million and interest has no doubt been paid over the last ten years, as this instance occurred some ten years ago. Not one house has been built, not one lot sold, not a single service provided in this area. We will need better planning than that particular effort in housing.
It is our view that by effective leadership in the field of housing the federal government could kill two birds with one stone. It could provide employment and at the same time reduce the cost of living for a basic essential of life, and incidentally improve the environment and living standards of many Canadians. We shall await with a great deal of interest how the government proposes to fill out the bare reference in the speech from the throne to amendments to the National Housing Act, because in our view this field

provides an important weapon to deal with the whole problem of unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, there is another urgent task for this parliament, I suggest, and that is its own revival as a vital institution. Those of us who are frank will have to admit to ourselves that parliament has fallen into disrepute. Very few Canadians look upon parliament with the respect they should. They fail to see in it an instrument to carry out the constructive plans and purposes which are essential. I think one reason for this low esteem of parliament is the inadequacy of the procedure of this house. For that reason I, and I think my colleagues in this party, welcome the proposal in the speech from the throne that a committee on procedure be established with the aim of strengthening parliament and making it more effective. I urge that this committee be taken seriously by all hon. members of this house and that the members of the committee and of this house do not shrink from radical changes where necessary. Such changes can, in my opinion, be brought about without in any way interfering with the basic rights of the members of this house.
I have on the order paper a resolution dealing with this particular subject, and I do not intend to discuss it in detail now. Unfortunately it is well down the order paper and I doubt if it will come up for quite a long time. I would, however, suggest that very high priority be given to making more effective use of the committee system. Unless that system is working the individual members of the house who are not members of the government cannot make the contribution of which they are capable. I was interested to note that exactly the same discussions are taking place on this matter in the British House of Commons, where they too are seeing the revival of parliament through an effective committee system in which all the members of that house have their part to play in gaining expert knowledge, in contributing to the particular subject on which they are qualified to contribute, and in carrying on the business of parliament in that way.
I also suggest that steps can be taken to eliminate repetitive debate, of which my short experience in the last house gave me quite a taste, and to provide for greater brevity in speeches. I am not worried so much about the private members as about the three-hour speeches which we occasionally hear from the leaders. I think we should endeavour to provide machinery, such as is provided in Sweden and New Zealand, to review and bring to the attention of this house invasions of individual rights by governmental or

bureaucratic action. I was very much encouraged by the Minister of Justice the other day when, in answer to a question, he suggested that the appointment of a parliamentary commissioner, known in Sweden as an ombudsman, would be considered by the committee on house procedure.
Amongst the other matters which are of great concern to my constituents as well as to all Canadians is a comprehensive system of contributory portable pensions, mentioned in the speech from the throne; also the subject of national health legislation or medicare, which was not mentioned. I suggest that this parliament will be judged by the people of Canada by the test of whether it is able to move ahead with other modern and civilized nations to effective legislation in both these spheres of contributory portable pensions and medicare. I do not propose to discuss medicare at this stage because my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton South, dealt with it very fully last Thursday.
Mr. Speaker, there is one other subject with which I wish to deal, and that is an aspect of Canada's external policies. I am glad the speech from the throne has recognized that Canada's economic progress is vitally dependant on vigorous economic progress and expansion throughout the world. It also recognizes the importance of pursuing active policies for the economic development of newer nations. The fact of the matter is that there has been a serious lack of balance as between the effort and thought that have gone into traditional aspects of defence, and the effort and thought that have gone into building a world community through a world strategy of economic development. This, I suggest, is equally important to the security of Canada as to the security of the world. This imbalance between the attention given to these two subjects is symbolized by the fact that Canada's contribution to what is known as economic aid is in the order of $70 million a year, in contrast to an expenditure of $1,650 million a year on traditional defence. The proportion therefore is that of one to 23.
I suggest that it is quite impossible to face the challenge of aggressive international communism by traditional methods of defence alone. They may be necessary, but in the field of economic aid the western world is lagging and Canada lags behind other sections of the western world.
Let us take a look for just a moment at the world in which we live. It is a world in which a part, namely the western world, has achieved by and large a dynamic economy which has gone far to abolish poverty and which can be justly described as an affluent
The Address-Mr. Brewin society. There are still many social injustices and much that has to be remedied, but the contrast between this affluent society and the abject poverty of two thirds of humanity is striking, and it has been growing. The sheer physical needs of the vast majority of the human race remain real, desperate and urgent. Much has been done but much more remains to be done.
The Marshall plan succeeded, through the infusion of large scale capital investment and the unparalleled generosity of the United States, in creating a viable and expanding economy in Europe which I suggest contributed as much as, if not more than, military defences, to the containment of communism. The economies of the underdeveloped countries in Asia, Africa and South America have not been devastated by war, but they too require the infusion of capital on a massive scale, on the same scale and with the same spirit that inspired the Marshall plan.
The speech from the throne recognizes this principle, because it says that the principles of Canadian external policy are those of the United Nations charter. The speech from the throne promises the promotion of the welfare of all peoples by international co-operation. I hope these words are not mere lip service as they too often have been in the past. At its fiftieth session the United Nations general assembly passed a resolution which among other things expressed the hope that the flow of international assistance and capital to developing countries would be increased substantially so as to reach as soon as possible approximately 1 per cent of the combined national income of the economically advanced countries. Canada's contribution to date has been in the order of one fifth of 1 per cent of our gross national product, so we are living up to one fifth of our obligations which the speech from the throne said we accept as the principles of Canadian external policy.
I hope this new government is going to do much better in this field, and we are going to keep an eye on what they propose to do. We will be watching very carefully to see whether the present government proposes to live up to the standards suggested in this important field by the United Nations, and to which the government has made reference in the speech from the throne.
I do not propose now to reopen the debate covered by the subamendment which was so narrowly defeated in the house the other day. I must say, though, that to me it is a tragic thing that Canada should not be leading the nations of the world away from the path of

The Address-Mr. Brewin nuclear dispersion which threatens the destruction of humanity. I find this particularly tragic because the decision of the government appears to have been based upon a view as to Canada's commitments which I find it difficult, if not impossible, to share. It certainly seems to me that if any commitment was made by Canada it was a commitment which was subject to review in the light of changing circumstances.
However that may be, I take comfort from the fact that the Prime Minister, in his famous Scarborough speech on January 11, said, and I have quotations from his speech:
How can Canada make her most effective contribution to collective security in order to avoid war?
That, he said, was the simple and basic defence question facing Canada. He then went on to make his own view, I thought, quite clear. He said:
The government should re-examine at once the whole basis ol Canadian defence policy. In particular it should discuss with the United States and with NATO a role for Canada in continental and collective defence, which would be more realistic and effective for Canada than the present one.
The present one is the one which the government is now purporting to carry out. The Prime Minister made it perfectly clear that we should at once, and these are his words, "reconsider that whole role at once". In the light of this the Prime Minister went on to make the following statement in his Scarborough speech:
The greatly increased power and range of nuclear missiles has also, paradoxically, increased the importance of non-nuclear conventional weapons. Cuba showed that. NATO is showing it...Western military thinking is therefore putting more emphasis on the strengthening of conventional forces. For smaller powers-
I take it we are one.
-this is economically the most feasible form of defence.
I call the Prime Minister to witness that even in his Scarborough speech on January 11 he said that the most feasible form of contribution to defence by Canada and by small nations such as Canada lies in the strengthening of conventional forces. I am also gratified that the Minister of National Defence made it clear that once the commitment which he believes was made by the former government is carried out, Canada should be able to pursue a non-nuclear role in the future. He contributed an article to The Varsity, a publication of the University of Toronto, in which he said:
One of the questions which bothers many sincere people is this: Will not the fulfilment of our commitments now make it impossible for us to pursue anything but a nuclear role in the future? The answer in my opinion is a resounding no.

This is the present Minister of National Defence speaking.
In the future we will be able to adopt the policy which we think is most in keeping with our national objectives.	_
He made it clear that he thought the policy most in keeping with our national objectives was one which would forgo the nuclear role and concentrate on conventional weapons. It is for this reason that we welcome the setting up of the committee to examine defence problems, and we hope it will proceed at once, as the Prime Minister has suggested, with a reappraisal of Canada's role in the light of up to date, strategic understanding and the needs of the western alliance. If this is done we are convinced that it will indicate a non-nuclear role for Canada and, indeed, a basic change in NATO's strategic policy.
May I summarize what I have endeavoured to say to the house in these remarks. I say this parliament can be noted for effective steps to modernize Canada's provisions for social security by medicare and a contributory portable pension. It can take the necessary steps to conquer mass unemployment. It can turn away from the path of nuclear involvement. It can make real and effective efforts to build a world community through a generous world strategy of economic aid and expanding trade.
Last but not least, this parliament can revive the fading prestige of parliament itself by businesslike and efficient procedure. This, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, is an inspiring time, and we in this party, and I am sure all other members of the house will contribute all we can to make this parliament effective in this way.

Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to congratulate you for having been unanimously chosen for the high position of Speaker of the house.
I trust that during this twenty sixth parliament, our conduct, as members of parliament, will not put an extra burden on your already heavy task.
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to find out about the scope that is allowed in a speech on a motion for an address to His Excellency in reply to the speech from the throne delivered by His Excellency the Administrator, a motion which, I believe everybody will agree, has been extremely well presented and supported by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) and the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette). On account of this scope, you will have to put up with a somewhat varied menu during the next few minutes.
My home town as well as the town where I now reside, are situated in the historical

county of Chateauguay, one of the three counties which make up the federal riding of Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie. I say it is a historical county because it is there that, exactly a century and a half ago this year, a small group of Canadian soldiers under Colonel de Salaberry, distinguished themselves in a military operation considered today by our military historians as the most important of the 1812-14 war. It was a military operation that definitely put an end to the efforts of the Americans who were trying to capture what was then the heart of Canada, the city of Montreal. If they had been successful in their efforts, the whole of Canada, after the capture of Montreal, would have surely and rapidly passed into American hands. Colonel de Salaberry, at the head of a military detachment mostly made up of French Canadians, drove back a much stronger American force in the main operation of the battle of Chateauguay. It gives me pleasure to point out here that several government departments have offered their co-operation so as to ensure a commemoration worthy of this important historical event.
As they had done when they helped England push back the army of Benedict Arnold several years before, the French Canadians at the time of the 1812-14 war recognized that it was to their mutual interest to help England to protect Canada against the forces from the south. It was unquestionably French Canada's loyalty which on October 26, 1813 prevented Canada from falling to the Americans. A hundred and fifty years later, I am convinced that it will precisely be the bicultural character of this country which will prevent Canada from losing its identity and simply becoming another state of our southern neighbours.
It was indeed comforting to learn from the speech from the throne that new and positive measures would be considered and introduced in order to preserve that alliance. The principles of freedom and equality which I think are endorsed by most Canadians must not be applied in a superficial manner or be simply ignored, but must rather make up the basis on which our two main groups, the French and the English, will find refuge, comfort and justice. If we want that status of equal partnership between the two mother races of our nation to be recognized and practised everywhere, terms and conditions will have to be brought into our constitutional regime.
But on the other hand we from Quebec must realize that the idea of an active bilingualism and biculturalism at the national level is something completely new for most
The Address-Mr. Ian Watson people in western Canada. I am sure that English speaking Canada will accept the changes which are necessary to maintain our nation as such, but the application of those changes will meet with difficulties unless they are presented with sound and reasonable conviction, free from any kind of ill-feeling or ultimatum.
It also gives me pleasure to note that our Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has announced that within two years, the project of a distinctive flag for Canada will be brought before this house for approval. I hope that when we adopt such a flag for our country, we will at the same time accept "O Canada" as our national anthem.
While the Chateauguay-Huntingdon-La-prairie riding is renowned for its apple orchards, its herds of pure bred milch cows and for the fact that it is the main milk supplier of the Montreal metropolitan area, that region, in view of its favourable geographic situation between the seaway and the American border, is bound to know a major industrial development. I am happy to note in the speech from the throne that this government is preparing legislation on regional planning and development. I want to stress that the area composed of St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville, Chambly-Rouville, Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie and Beauharnois counties have a potential for industrial development unsurpassed anywhere else in Canada. The American region south of our area, made up of northern New England and New York states, is a rather undeveloped or underdeveloped area as compared with the American area which lies right to the south of industrialized Ontario. I think that it would be possible with adequate planning and a skillful use of our assets, such as our surplus power, for the triangle composed of the southwestern part of the province of Quebec to become, in a more or less distant future, a major industrial centre serving a large portion of the northern part of the New England and New York states, with the help perhaps of some tariff agreements.

Mr. Speaker, when I left off this morning I had just completed saying that I hope the government will eventually decide to establish a special wing of the national research council, staffed with planning scientists who will be able to plan for all our needs 25 to 50 years hence.
We realize that most of the area in which this planning will be involved comes within provincial jurisdiction, but I suggest that this special wing of the national research council should have on its staff at least one or two town planners and architects of world wide reputation and that, at the request of municipalities and regional bodies, they should be able to supply plans for the long range development of a particular region with regard to industry, culture, recreation, health and accommodation. I am convinced that Canada needs such a group of theoretical planners if we are to avoid in the future the mistakes resulting from the lack of regional planning which have so characterized our past.
The constituency of Chateauguay-Hunting-don-Laprairie is approximately two thirds agricultural, with dairying predominant as the major farm industry. This dairy industry is faced with two immediate and serious problems. The first is the campaign of the Montreal dairies and the refrigeration industry to force all milk producers in the Montreal milkshed to adopt bulk refrigeration units at a cost of at least $2,000 per farm. As I have heard rumours that some United States areas which have adopted these units are not satisfied with the results, 1 feel that our Department of Agriculture should launch an immediate, impartial inquiry into the economic benefits resulting from the introduction of these bulk units, and I have sent a letter to the Minister of Agriculture asking him to do just that.
The second problem is the removal of the 25 cents per hundredweight subsidy on fluid milk shipped to butter factories. This has adversely affected many farmers in my constituency. Although the subsidy on milk shipped to cheese factories has been increased by 30 cents per hundredweight, few 
cheese factories exist; and although the theory behind this move, which is that of switching milk from the production of butter, which we cannot sell, to the production of cheese which we can sell, is correct, unnecessary hardship is being caused.
I suggest that the Department of Agriculture aid butter factories that wish to change to cheese production, by providing through other government agencies the necessary credit for such changeovers. This would go a long way toward alleviating the immediate hardship and toward achieving the end result desired, which is decreased butter production and increased cheese production.
Mr. Speaker, there are approximately 10,000 Mohawk Indians living on two reservations, Caughnawaga and St. Regis, located within my constituency. These people are extremely dissatisfied with the present Indian Act, to the extent that less than a dozen voted in the last general election. The application of the same rules and regulations to Indians living in Montreal suburbia and to Indians living in the Hudson bay marshlands is absurd and antiquated. I shall go into this subject in greater detail at a later date, but let it suffice for the moment for me to state it is to be hoped the government will undertake a complete revision and modernization of the Indian Act.
The question of nuclear arms has special significance to the population of the counties of Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie. At Champlain, New York, 1,000 feet from my constituency; at Mooers Forks, one and a half miles from my constituency; at Ellenburg Depot, one and a half miles from my constituency, and at Chateauguay, New York, two miles from my constituency are located four hard site offensive Atlas missile sites. The location of these sites, 300 feet underground and within 35 miles of approximately 2 million Canadians living in the Montreal region, guarantees the immediate total destruction of those counties, together with the population of the Montreal area, within the first few minutes of a nuclear conflict regardless of whether Canada remains neutral or otherwise.
To the population of my constituency it makes absolutely no sense to be complaining about defensive Bomarc missiles 300 and 400 miles away from population centres when offensive missiles exist on their very doorstep, guaranteeing their annihilation in the first minutes of any war. Because we sit in the very shadow of those offensive weapons I think we realize better than many Canadians why Canada must co-operate completely in any defensive measures which will make war less likely.
The members of the New Democratic party have argued that Canada can only have an

effective voice in the world, especially among the so-called uncommitted nations, if we refuse to have anything to do with nuclear arms, but surely is it not our special relationship with our southern neighbour which gives the voice of Canada a special position in the world chorus? If this special relationship deteriorates because of our unwillingness to co-operate in the defence of this continent which we share with the United States, then surely the voice of Canada becomes less effective, whether it be in the councils of disarmament or in expounding the view of the uncommitted nations on a particular subject.
This parliament is facing many difficult problems. The right hon. Prime Minister has already indicated that he is tackling these problems energetically and decisively. I would hope that in solving these problems we would not fear taking good advice from our adversaries, and that our guiding formula will be that for each problem a solution exists which is better than any other. This best solution can be found if we gather adequate facts and undertake proper analysis.
Finally, I would hope that once this best solution is determined it will be put into effect without fear-should it mean more government control or planning-of the myth that all government control and planning is evil; and if the particular solution should lie in less government interference and the encouragement of private capital, I hope it will be effected without fear of hurting the feelings of our socialistic friends.

I express these words with a sincerity which is no less than when I conveyed my congratulations personally. I know that the judgment from that quarter is in good hands. Although I cannot agree with everything they said, they did justice to the task that was given them.
I notice, Mr. Speaker, that on the list of speakers for today we have the hon. lady from Winnipeg South (Mrs. Konantz), whom I certainly look forward to hearing. Although it may not be evident to the hon. lady, I have noticed that she is a very distinguished person and has deported herself well since her arrival in this house. I might say that she bears a certain resemblance to the first hon. lady to sit in this House of Commons, one of my predecessors. I think the opportunity that awaits the hon. lady from Winnipeg South is much greater than awaited my
The Address-Mr. Winkler predecessor-although she will do well to equal her performance-because I recall very well that when the Liberal party decided that Miss Agnes Macphail had occupied her seat for too long, at the time of redistribution the stroke of a pen eliminated her for all time from this house.
As other hon. members have stated in their maiden speeches, I too, after my fourth election to this house, appreciate the honour bestowed upon one so humble as myself in being sent here as a representative of my constituency and of Canada. I hope the hon. members who have made such eloquent addresses will not be disillusioned in the years to come by their participation in this chamber. Certainly this has not been the case so far with myself, and I hope this attitude will not change. I came here in 1957 to represent the people of my constituency and, indeed, all Canadians. I came here to represent all those in my constituency regardless of their political affiliations. I have endeavoured to do this justly, wisely and to the best of my ability. I hope this will remain in the minds of hon. gentlemen who have delivered addresses in this chamber for the first time.
I note, however, regrettably that the old signs of patronage are already becoming evident. This is regrettable when we realize that this is the machine which ran our country prior to 1957. Indeed, just the other day-and I regret that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is not here-we noted the first of these acts in the removal of Brigadier John H. Price from his position at the United Nations, where he had served Canada well and in a distinguished manner. I can only suggest to the members of the government that this will do nothing but harm to our status in that world federation. I regret this. I do not hesitate to suggest that this type of action is becoming evident within the limits of my constituency. Since my entry into this chamber there has never at any time been any member in the government service from my constituency who has not had my support. This applies to any institution of or any position in the government which is within the boundaries of Grey-Bruce.
However, I have now noticed so early in the life of this government that it is becoming evident that the old machine that was very creaky from disuse is getting some oil at the necessary joints. I regret to see this. Not only is it happening in my constituency, but we have had evidence of this in other quarters. I warn hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly those who occupy the back benches, that they would do well to see that such practices are not again put into effect as they were prior to 1957.

The Address-Mr. Winkler
It may be that the new era of Liberal control suggested in the Globe and Mail of May 23 is becoming a reality. The article in this newspaper is headed "A tighter rein on the Liberals". I believe that such a tight rein ruled prior to 1957, and as I have said, this is once again becoming evident. I do not believe that the Prime Minister himself is responsible for this, but it is under the direction of his chief lieutenant, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). Under his control all these things will be enforced. I also believe that the program and strategy that was used to bring the Prime Minister to his present high office was directed and controlled by the Secretary of State. I shall attempt to prove this in a very few minutes.
Before I get into the area of that argument, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that the constituency I represent is probably the hub of the furniture industry in the Dominion of Canada. I recall that in the days prior to 1957, even with the protection of a 22i per cent tariff these people had a very difficult time competing with the big industrial machine of our neighbour to the south. The 22J per cent protection was not enough to discourage imports into this country, and as a result this industry was placed in a very depressed condition. Through the actions of the Conservative government these people realized full employment and prosperity. They had never seen such prosperity. When I hear of the free trade program which is likely to come into being, the slashing of tariffs, I can only say to my constituents "Beware", because this is the warning I put forward during the election campaign. Even with this tariff this industry does not compete very well now, even though they have spent millions of dollars to bring themselves in line with automation and current day production methods It will be an even more difficult thing if this tariff is tampered with for these people to stay in business, as was the case prior to 1957.
However, there is one glimmer of hope which I would extend to the people of my constituency and any other constituency which has this industry within its bounds. That is that the Prime Minister has made a statement -and I have it here-to the effect that we do want some exceptions. I will hang my hat on that very small nail, hoping that when this new program becomes effective the Prime Minister and his government will see that this industry does not pass into oblivion, as we expect will be the case with other smaller secondary industries.
My constituency is also partly rural, and this causes me to consider the activities of the government in regard to that smaller agricultural industry. They are taking a great


deal of joy out of the fact that they are now saving $6 million from the payment of subsidies to milk producers. We all realized that something had to be done, but I do believe this has been done to the disadvantage of the small farmer, the man we decided we would support. These people, too, come into the same category as the industrial furniture workers to whom I have referred. My job since I came here has been to stand up for these people in the smaller income categories, and I will continue to fight for them until they say they do not want me any longer. But at the present rate it will be a long, long time before they say that.
As I suggested earlier, the days of patronage seem to be returning. After what was said prior to and during the election campaign I believe this may be a necessary area for the government to move into, but if they return to their former practices they will be put into the street in short order, because I do not think the people of this country will stand for it very long. One thing I know definitely is that the people of Grey-Bruce will stand behind me with regard to the attitude I have taken toward public institutions and for the efforts I have made on behalf of those in the lower income brackets. That is the way I intend to continue, and I suggest my seat will be very secure if present indications of what might happen do come to pass. I cannot be more specific than that; the ministers concerned will know whereof I speak.
It is necessary for me to say a few things, first of all, as to the economy of the country prior to the change of government. I do not think there is anyone in this country, even in the Liberal party, who would suggest we were having anything but prosperity and good times. Yet the hon. lady from Northumberland suggested we must do something to get the economy rolling. That is a fine thing, of course. I can recall one occasion, last New Year's I think it was, when the present Prime Minister told us that one of his New Year's resolution, if he were returned to power, would be to get rid of unemployment. Canadians, he said, could expect something better out of the economy. Well, he may be right, but he had better check with the Minister of Trade and Commerce; because, speaking in Vancouver on February 20, that hon. gentleman said Canada could never eliminate unemployment. There are a number of other contradictory statements with which the right hon. gentleman will have to deal.
As for the Prime Minister himself, he and his whole party planned to kill the last parliament; they planned to destroy it and bring to an end any co-operation which existed in that twenty fifth parliament. All we have to

do to confirm this is look at what he said in the house on October 1, 1962, as reported on page 74 of Hansard of that date. Listen to this:
We have heard a good deal in recent weeks- a good deal more in recent days-of the necessity of putting the national interests above the playing of politics.
We all know what went on. We know what the circumstances were. Members opposite say there was no obstruction, but we know better. Anyone who sat in this house knows this to be the case. The right hon. gentleman went on to say:
That talk does not come very convincingly to me at least, from those whose concern to avoid an appeal to the people could preserve a state of political weakness and uncertainty such as we have in this parliament today.
In other words he blamed us, in that brief parliament of 1962, because we would not go to the people. I will tell you why he wanted us to go, Mr. Speaker. It was because of a direct design on the part of the present Secretary of State and his minions to destroy the prime minister of the day, discredit parliament and go back to the people on bogus charges. During the campaign the people were told up and down the country that the Conservative government had been spending too much money and was putting Canada into bankruptcy. This statement was repeated time and time again. Yet here is a statement which appared in the Globe and Mail of April 18, 1961, shortly after the Liberal party convention at the Chateau Laurier. It begins:
In promising a miraculous cure for Canada's economic ills, the Liberal party appears to be basing its seven point program of pre-election lures on the assumption that people not only can, but actually want to be fooled.
Well, if the Liberal party ever invoke the promises made at that convention they will see what a broke country looks like in comparison with the good order and high degree of prosperity which existed when the former government left office.
Certainly the former government was ready to spend money. What government with half a brain in its head would not have spent money on coming to office in 1957? There was no one happier to get rid of the responsibility of office at that time than the leader of the Liberal party and those associated with him, and no one more capable to restore conditions of prosperity than we on this side of the house.
Let us look to the United States to see what the situation is there. In the United States, with unemployment numbering 5 million, President Kennedy has proposed to budget for a deficit of $10.3 billion. I think hon. members opposite would be well advised to
The Address-Mr. Winkler realize this, because in view of the promises they have made some definite action will be necessary. The people of this country will probably be looking to a balanced budget. We shall await action by hon. members opposite and see what their magic will be as this program gets rolling.
It will not be for us on this side to obstruct the business before us. I think we have deported ourselves very well already. Certainly the government will have my co-operation in this regard though it is a difficult thing for them, after what they did last year, to realize that anyone in this house can be responsible. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, and the people of this country, precisely what happened. Let us go back to February 24, 1962. When commenting on a speech by the present Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin), one of the Toronto newspapers said the activities of the house had reached "a new low level". I do not have to repeat for the benefit of hon. members what was said on that occasion, but it was one of the most despicable speeches I have ever heard. I can recall another occasion when we read the report of a speech delivered in Toronto by the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), in which he called the then prime minister dishonest. I think, too, of December 19 last when the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) was responsible for shouting down the prime minister of the day.
Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, what the plan was. It was a deliberate plan, made years before April 8, to destroy the product, which is Canada, to destroy the nerve centre, which is parliament, and then buy it back cheaply. This was the plan of hon. members who now support the government. I shall wait to see the operation of this patronage pattern take effect in order to have verified exactly what I have said. The people of my riding will get the words of this address, and I am the first to say I will back everything I have said. The government and its supporters may disagree, but we are all too well aware of what happened.
I travel now closer to the present day. I think the Liberal party is indeed fortunate to be manning the government benches on that side of the house. I say this in the light of newspaper articles predicting that the next boom will be bigger than the last one regardless of what government sits in Ottawa. This, I believe, is a *well known fact among economists who have made predictions in the last few weeks. But somebody had to bring our affairs to this point, and it was a government under the direction of the Conservative party which did it. They certainly took into hand the circumstances which

The Address-Mr. Winkler existed in 1957 and brought us out of a recession which the Grits were proud to wash their hands of.
Then I think, Mr. Speaker, of the charges which were made with regard to obstructionism in the last parliament, and how they continued them on the hustings. I suggest that we read the words of an editorial in the Globe and Mail of April 15, 1963. This is the Globe and Mail after the election campaign-and I repeat the Globe and Mail, Mr. Speaker:
But the opposition-
They are referring to the Liberal party.
-did waste some time and did interfere with the orderly conduct of parliament. The country will be in no mood for a similar performance during the coming parliament.
We believe this, and as a result we will certainly not put on the display that these people put on in the last parliament. If parliament reached a low, Mr. Speaker, we all know who was responsible for it, and there is certainly no question about that statement.
Then I think of a few other things which happened in the course of the election campaign. I think of the words of the present Prime Minister when he said on February 6 that he did not expect to see the election result in no party having a very clear majority in the house, but that if it did all leaders would have to search their conscience and come to the aid of their country. That is what he said in answer to a question from a newsman.
Mr. Speaker, after all the instances I have quoted I should think that the report by Mr. Lubor Zink of the Toronto Telegram, would be more apt in this regard. Mr. Zink reported that the present Prime Minister did not win a clear majority, when he and the present leader of the government-that is the prime minister of that day-
-should resign to let the two parties work together for the good of the country.
I have heard nothing of that one, although I realize that the present Prime Minister denied that statement later on. Then Mr. Zink, who is no particular friend of this party, went on to say down the line that one or two more lies would not matter anyway. I do not know what he was referring to, but it was in direct relation to that particular question.
Mr. Speaker, it has become evident that we are not going to be terribly concerned about the economic level of this country unless this situation is tampered with. Therefore, if there is any increase in the number of undesirable areas with which we have to deal in this house, we will also be able to put the responsibility for them directly on

the shoulders of this government; and, as I said, they will have my support so far as this parliament is concerned.
Because the speech from the throne is always couched in generalities we cannot refer to very many specific points. That is the purpose of a debate like this, so that we can deal with a wide range of subjects. The subject which interested me was the reference to a municipal loan fund. I am all in favour of such a fund, and I would support it. But the way the Liberal party has projected this idea is, I believe, somewhat different from what the country would expect. I do not for one moment think the country would expect the Liberal government to stay within their support of Social Credit's interest free money, such as the Minister of Finance suggested last year. I do not think that will be the case. But until I see the terms of this bill I will possess my soul in patience and wait for the bill to come forward.
Mr. Speaker, I will tell you why. The winter works program which was projected by the previous minister of labour I believe was superior to the municipal loan fund which is to come forward. The interest rate will have to be extremely low or the municipalities will not be in any different position than they are today. Mr. Speaker, look at the winter works program which was under the administration of the former minister of labour. It contributed directly to the financial support of the communities through the support which we offered to the municipalities if their projects were accepted.
In the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, we will wait and see what the legislative program will be. I am satisfied that as the days go by this party on this side of the house will deport itself and discharge its responsibilities in accordance with what I have stated. We will wait for the legislative program and do our utmost to see that the responsibility of opposition so far as the country is concerned is maintained to a much higher degree in this parliament than it was in the twenty fifth parliament of Canada.
