Mr. Speaker, last week the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Girouard) and the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) made some rather crafty remarks concerning me. That is why I am participating in this debate. I shall be as brief, concise and calm as hon. members on this side of the house have been in the past few days when they have addressed the house.

However, as I would not want to break well established traditions, it is most natural that I should congratulate all those whom the house has honoured lately.
My riding is one of the most typical and, at the same time, one of the most beautiful in the province of Quebec and in Canada. As everybody knows, it is partly urban and partly rural; it is also typical of the whole of Canada in that it is becoming increasingly industrial and urban.
An American sociologist, Mr. Hughes, looking for the most representative city in the province of Quebec for the purpose of his book entitled "French Canada in Transition", chose the city of Drummondville.
Drummond-Arthabaska is a county where secondary industry, based on the textile and furniture industries, is experiencing all the ups and downs to which it is subjected throughout Canada, and where agriculture, dependant on milk production to a very great extent, is in almost permanent difficulties.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, it is a county which contains a sprinkling of Anglo-Saxons among a mainly French speaking population. Therefore, the problems raised by the relations between French speaking and English speaking Canadians and by federal-provincial relations take on in this riding an unusual meaning. There is a tremendous interest in those problems.
During the recent election campaign it was even said: as goes Drummond-Arthabaska, so will the whole of Quebec go. Mr. Speaker, you will admit that such a typical riding, such a representative riding must have an excellent representation here and that is what I intend to give in the years to come.
Mr. Speaker, for the next 25 years I intend to frequently talk about the problems most dear to my heart, problems which interest me passionately, problems of international relations, of constitutional law, and economic, social and farm problems.
At this stage of my remarks, I should like to say by the way that I am not an economist. I have the greatest respect and admiration for the economists, but I am not one of them,
I belong to this new category of sociologists called "politologists". This could be a word to add to the vocabulary of this house where the future of politologists is bright because they are already represented in this house by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett), whom I wish to commend for
The Address-Mr. Pepin her excellent contribution to this debate, and also by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie).
Politologists are interested in everything. Their eagerness to find out things is uncommon, as I hope to show you in the years to come.
In England, we find in the letters to the editors the phrase "student of politics". Well, Mr. Speaker, I shall be, in this house, a "student of politics".
I intend today to talk about things I may know the least, which will give my hon. friend from St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) an opportunity to say, like so many others, that I am talking through my hat.
There is a danger for me in doing this, but it may be the wise thing to do because the quality of my remarks cannot but improve as compared to my effort of today, and the press will be able to say: the young member for Drummond-Arthabaska is improving daily.
I shall refer therefore to an agricultural matter, especially that of the dairy industry, because it is an important problem for all of Canada, for the whole province of Quebec and particularly for my constituency, an important problem also for my party. In the months and years to come, the Liberal party will absolutely have to improve the agricultural situation in the east. That is a must, if we are to establish the equality we hope for and want between eastern and western farmers, that equality which did not exist in the past, as can be easily demonstrated. We shall try to remedy the situation. That is why, in the speech from the throne, great importance is given to the appointment of a minister of agriculture for eastern Canada. And yet some members of the opposition have ridiculed the idea.
There is no question of impoverishing western farmers but simply to better the lot of eastern farmers. A formula used recently by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) about GATT can be taken up again here: a balance of advantages is imperative.
Here is something the hon. members for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot and Nicolet-Yamaska could do, they could convince their own colleagues of the importance of that matter, instead of wasting their time laughing at those who, like me, consider it very important.

That is what we call a tempest in a teapot.
So I intend to deal with the decision made by the government on April 29 last to cancel the 25-cent per 100 pounds subsidy on milk that is paid to processing plants. Why this decision? Why the cancellation of that subsidy? To fight the very detrimental effects of the subsidy policy of the previous government, that led to the stockpiling of 200 million pounds of butter in warehouses. This when the federal government had the opportunity to sell cheese, powdered milk and casein, when it could have sold on the foreign market between 5 and 6 million pounds of cheese, when half our consumption of fancy cheese was imported. So we had to give this policy a new direction.
The hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska- you will excuse me if I refer to him-says that he is in favour of planning, but as soon as action in that direction is contemplated, he condemns it, probably because he is selfassertive. In my opinion, he has not yet discovered the meaning of that word.
Our purpose was therefore to guide production, to discourage butter production without weakening it, to stimulate cheese and casein production because there was a market for those products.
Why did we act so fast? Why was a decision taken in four days? I wondered myself. The answer is that the Agricultural Stabilization Act required a yearly revision, otherwise we would have gone on producing butter and, adding to the 200 million pounds I mentioned before.
If we had pursued the policy of the previous administration, at the end of the year the members of the opposition could have told us: "Where is the planning the Liberal party was talking about?" And they would have blamed us for not taking that decision at that time.
It is also important, Mr. Speaker, to point out that such a decision was taken with the agreement of the representative dairy producers' organizations, the Catholic Farmers'

Union, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the National Dairy Council, the Canadian Milk Producers Association. All those organizations supported that step. This is giving a commendable importance to intermediate bodies, to representative organizations, in matters concerning them.
Now, what have we done on April 29 to promote cheese production? We maintained the support price for cheese at 32J cents and we raised stabilization grants from 25 to 30 cents per hundredweight of milk going into Cheddar production. Then, as far as cheese production is concerned, we thought that fancy cheeses were able to move along and find their own way to the domestic and foreign markets.
On the other hand, so that butter production might not be unduly affected, the government deemed it proper to increase the 12 cent subsidy paid previously on every pound of butter to 14J cents per pound of butter fat.
That is a point on which the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska disagrees with the experts other than himself. He claimed that such a decision would result in a loss of $817 for every parish in his riding. And everybody knows now that there are 32.
It seems that the calculations made so carefully by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska is erroneous. He makes his calculations on the basis that 100 pounds of fat are equivalent to 122J pounds of butter. Now, according to experts from the Department of Agriculture, this is not so. There are 100 pounds of fat on an average for 121 pounds of butter. In my riding, some even say 117.
I do not think it is necessary to appoint a royal commission to determine which experts are right. If you multiply 100 pounds of fat by 14J cents, you get $14.50 whereas 121 pounds of butter at 12 cents gives $14.52. Therefore, it comes to the same thing.
As far as powdered milk is concerned, it is true that the 25 cents stabilization subsidy has been abolished but the government will buy large quantities of powdered milk with the result that prices will go up. It will pay 11 cents a pound for it instead of the current price of 8 cents or 8J cents a pound.
Such a step should bring about a price hike as the newspaper La Presse stated on May 24, 1963:
It follows that while producers will lose the subsidy on processed milk, they will benefit from the rise on the price of powdered milk and the companies and co-operatives will increase the price of processed milk accordingly. Experts feel that
The Address-Mr. Pepin this increase will compensate for the loss of the subsidy.
As far as casein is concerned, a product used for the manufacturing of plastics, we export it to the extent of 90 per cent. Therefore, a subsidy of 10 cents a pound will work to the advantage of the producers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the butter, cheese and milk producers will have to let their suppliers share in the advantages they get. I am glad to be able to quote from a letter I received this morning from the Granby farm cooperative:
If you compare the price paid in the last two weeks of April to the price members will get for the first two weeks of May, you will see that for those periods there is no difference in our case. The price for milk has not changed-
Mr. Speaker, is that a good policy? It is held to be good by the experts and the organizations concerned. At least, it is better than what was going on before, when the heap of butter was left to grow and grow.
I honestly believe it is too early to judge. The days to come will tell us what the results of that policy will be. No doubt there is room for improvement. We are the first to deplore the fact that this initial step the Department of Agriculture had to take for eastern Canada cannot please everybody.
But what does that prove? Well, it proves the need for a minister of agriculture for eastern Canada, to look after the interests of eastern farmers.
It also proves the need for a global policy, a comprehensive policy for eastern agriculture.
It also proves the need to find new uses for milk, whether it be the fattening up of school children or the fattening up of livestock. I apologize for putting both in the same category.
It proves among other things, as the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott (Mr. Ethier) said, the need to improve agricultural conditions.
It proves the necessity of an over-all agricultural policy, a rational one, and especially of a policy concerning feed grains.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, it is not enough to have vision, or visions, we sometimes need prevision. Sometimes we must do some planning, and we just inherited the situation created by the lack of agricultural planning of the previous government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I assure you it is more than just an amenity to congratulate you on having been chosen for the high position which you presently occupy and to wish you the greatest degree of satisfaction in that position, because I am sure those are the sentiments of your many friends in this chamber. May I say also


that those sentiments apply equally to the Speaker and the chairman of committees.
At this stage I should like also to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. This is the first opportunity that I have had to congratulate them. I feel that they performed their duties in a way that would bring satisfaction to their constituents, and I am sure they brought credit to themselves in this house in the process.
I would like now to mention that the speech delivered by His Excellency the Administrator, contains many suggestions which are thought provoking to all in this chamber. But Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who believe that a nation is only as great as the people who compose its citizenship. I am one who believes in the development of the individual. I believe in the encouragement of his creative instincts and his desire to accomplish things. I believe in the encouragement of his desire to work, and his ambition to acquire a stake in his country, his native land, as a result of effort, long hours of work, and determination.
The talented hon. lady who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne stated categorically that we have moved from an individualistic society to a collectivist society, and then she proceeded to state that the Liberal party is quite prepared to accept that proposition. I shall quote her own very words:
I think the party, or most members within the party at any rate, are prepared to accept this growth toward a collectivist society that we have witnessed and furthermore-and this is even more important-are prepared to accept the argument that such a society can simply not be selfregulated, that such a society does require direction and guidance from the main institutions that the people have to help them, namely governments at all levels, municipal, provincial and federal.
I submit that the question can properly be asked, where does this put the Liberal party? How far to the left does it bring it? In my opinion it brings it close to the socialist camp because I assume the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) expresses the policy of the Liberal party.
It is my opinion that direction and guidance should go from individuals to government, and not from government to individuals. I am unable to agree that we have completely moved to a collectivist society, but I am prepared to acknowledge that the throne speech contains indications of future action by this government which may lead to the condition she envisages as having arrived. Let me first state that governments by their action and by their emphasis can contribute to the development of the individual, or otherwise

but I believe that the individual, by his or her accomplishments, should be the foundation of our society.
The function of government is not to make people happy, but to create the opportunity by which they may make themselves happy. In several places in the first part of the throne speech there appears the word "opportunity". It refers to new opportunities and expanding opportunities, and I like those words. It is good for people to consider that it is opportunity which is important to all of us, to our society, to our young people, indeed to all our people. In this connection I wish to quote two paragraphs from the throne speech:
You are deliberating the course of our country in times of great change throughout the world. These are times that test old virtues. They are times that open up new opportunities. Familiar ways of thought and action are becoming less certain guides. The task before us is to seek out. with wisdom and imagination, those new paths that will lead us surely forward.
No one in this chamber could disagree with that paragraph. The next paragraph reads:
As Canadians we can work with hope. Our country has a proud history. Now there are expanding opportunities open to us. But they depend on our overcoming serious problems. It is only with courage and perseverance and hard work that we will achieve the better life that is within our power, for ourselves and for our children.
Our progress is the work of all the people. In a free country, we are all responsible.
Mr. Speaker, in seeking out the new paths which the throne speech states will surely lead us forward, it is my contention that we cannot discard the old virtues and the old attributes which have contributed to our progress, both individually and as a nation over the years.
There is much in the new which we should acquire. This is in fact the Conservative philosophy-the preservation of all that is useful of the past, and the acquisition of the new ideas that make for progress. Those were the guiding principles of the Conservative government from June 1957 to April 1963, a period of nearly six years. Let us look and see what happened during that period of time.
I have before me a condensation of what took place under various general headings. Dealing first with the gross national product, under the Conservative government it increased from $30,500,000,000 to $40,400,000,000, an increase of 32.74 per cent in those six years. Labour income increased from $14,800,000,000 to $20,300,000,000, an increase of 36.72 per cent. Personal income in 1956 stood at $21,800,000,000, and by 1962 it had risen to $30,700,000,000, an increase of 40.70 per cent. Retail trade in 1956 totalled $1,192,000,000,
The Address-Hon. H. J. Flemming and in 1962 it was $1,455,000,000, an increase of 22.06 per cent. Steel production, which is sometimes used as a measuring stick for development in any nation, rose from 5,301,000 tons to 7,174,000 tons in the same period, an increase of 35.33 per cent. United States tourist expenditure in Canada rose from $309,000,000 in 1956 to $510,000,000 in 1962, an increase of 65.04 per cent. Overseas tourists spent $28 million in 1956 as compared with $50 million in 1962, an increase of 78.57 per cent, and the number of U.S. tourists who came to Canada increased from 27,700,000 to 31,700,000, an increase of 14.44 per cent.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the accomplishments of a government working with the philosophy I have just mentioned, the philosophy of keeping what is good of the old and picking up what is useful of the new for progress in the future. The results which I have read are tremendously impressive and, as I say, they are the results of Conservative government.
The speech from the throne also states that the ministers will expand Canada's export trade. I can tell them how to do it. Let them just consult the Leader of the Opposition as to how to accomplish this since, under his government, the excess of imports over exports prevailing when the Liberals left office was completely eliminated. From a figure of $713 million unfavourable balance on merchandise account in 1957, the position was changed to a favourable balance for 1961 of $173 million, and for 1962 of $155 million. If you add the two figures together you will find the net difference was close to a billion dollars in that period of time.
I suggest to the government that the intention of setting up more departments, more boards and the establishment of more ministries and councils is something which is not acceptable to the people of Canada who have the responsibility of paying the bills. The proliferation of bureaucracy is something which in my opinion should be frowned upon and not encouraged. The funds for the payment of much needless duplication must come from taxes and the apparently forgotten man, the taxpayer. There is in Canada today an opinion that there is more volume of bureaucracy than is necessary. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) might tell the house what the annual cost will be of the various departments, boards, councils, etc. forecast in the speech from the throne. In his budget speech he will be obliged to tell the house where he expects to find the money to pay the bill.
Mr. Speaker, I now wish to refer to unemployment for a few minutes. All hon. members will agree, I am sure, with the speech from the throne when it states that this is
37$

The Address-Hon. H. J. Flemming the most urgent of our domestic problems. Much has been said about it in this debate, and we are all concerned about this problem. I am convinced that in the final analysis there is only one method of attacking this problem which has any chance of being successful; that is, for government and industry to tackle the problem by working together at it. A solution will not be found by setting up more and more government departments. A solution may be found by encouraging industry to create employment. A man who works for industry is a producer. In this connection may I say, Mr. Speaker, that I believe quite impressive progress was made between the years 1961 and 1962. I find that the labour force in Canada between those two years increased from 6.5 million, in round figures, to 6.7 million, which is an increase of 2.8 per cent. I also find that during this same period employment for all months on the average increased by 4.1 per cent. This is the comment which Canadian Business Service Limited makes in this connection:
Reflecting the sharp increase in national output, employment rose by 4.1 per cent to 6.3 million thus exceeding the 2.8 per cent increase in the labour force by a considerable margin, with the result that the number of unemployed dropped appreciably from an average rate of 7.2 per cent of the labour force in 1961 to 6.4 per cent in 1962.
Mr. Speaker, the minister of labour of the previous government is in his seat, and I think he deserves a major portion of the credit for that improved result. This government has announced its intention of expanding its bureaucracy. It is my opinion that they should make more use of the many splendid men and women now available in the public service, rather than adding to it. There is too much tendency in government to establish entities which compete with private enterprise, too much application of Parkinson's law, too little use of services which could be performed by private industry, too much tendency to be competitive with industry, too little tendency to be co-operative.
I find that among some influential people in government service there seems to be impatience sometimes almost bordering on contempt of free enterprise and private industry. Where there should be a tendency to encourage, there sometimes seems to be a desire to hinder. Where there should be a tendency to be conciliatory, it sometimes seems there is a desire to be tough. Where there should be a tendency to co-operate, it seems to me there is very often a tendency to compete. I consider that the private enterpriser is entitled to the respect of the government, who is his partner and in many


cases receives about 50 per cent of his profits. While on the subject of profits, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that in my opinion it is profits which are responsible for the payment of bills for the many things which we consider important. None of us would ever receive a cheque for services were it not for taxes resulting from profits. I think the word "profit" should be one of the most highly respected words in the English language. Moreover, it is the measuring stick of an efficient performance. It takes no ability to spend government money. It takes no ability to spend any kind of money, for that matter. Anyone can do it; I can do it. But it does take ability to conduct a successful business, make profits and pay a large percentage as a contribution to general public expenditure, welfare costs and other activities. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said regarding unemployment, that it is by co-operation and not competition with private industry that governments can have any hope of grappling successfully with the existing situation.
But what do we find this government proposing in the speech from the throne? We find them proposing two ministers of agriculture, and the transfer of the administration of the wheat board to the Department of Trade and Commerce. Are we to assume that this means a tremendous increase in personnel, with the substantial costs resulting from it? They propose to augment the Atlantic development board, already set up with a representative of each Atlantic province, with six extra members. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this is a definite political gimmick designed to clip the wings of the existing personnel when it comes to a vote. I wonder how the Atlantic provinces Liberal members can possibly favour this, because if they do it represents their acceptance of the principle of divide and conquer, which was in operation as long as I can remember until the coming into office of the Diefenbaker government in 1957. I will have a little more to say about that when the resolution is before the house.
I take exception to the use of the word "strengthen" in the speech from the throne referring to the Atlantic development board. They should have used the word "lengthen" because that is all they are doing; they are just going to lengthen it to a membership of 11. So far as the capital fund is concerned, I submit that this compares most unfavourably with the plan envisaged by the original act. I submit that the government has no right to delegate the spending of $100 million or any other amount without coming before parliament for approval. The act as originally constituted and passed contemplated that all the resources of Canada would be at the disposal

The Address-Hon. H. J. Flemming and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Des-ehatelets) had confirmed that federal assistance would be available for trunk roads.
My comment is this: it appears strange that announcements as important as these and having such extensive financial implications would not be made in the House of Commons rather than in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal, even though the latter is an excellent newspaper. Perhaps the Prime Minister will explain.
The speech states that the ministers have undertaken to establish a comprehensive system of contributory pensions. This is simply carrying out an expressed intention of the previous government and I have no hesitation whatever in saying that I favour it strongly, as I did when our government was considering it. I favoured it strongly then. The very fact that the present government is carrying out .our expressed intention is most satisfactory and pleasing. The plan suggests contributions by people at an early age, contributions which would continue until the retirement of those concerned. I would point out that this is an encouragement of thrift and saving, two of the old virtues mentioned in the speech from the throne. We shall await with anticipation the submission of the details.
In conclusion, may I submit to this government the admonition that they will do extremely well if, in future, they maintain the progress made by their predecessors. They might well adopt the slogan, "Continue to go forward" as we were going forward prior to April 8.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in making my first speech in this house, I do not feel among strangers, having been associated with many members in public endeavours for some years. The historic role of this house must impress all who sit here, and particularly those of us who are most junior resolve to use its privileges and perform its duties with responsibility. May I add my word of congratulation to you, Mr. Speaker, upon your election to high office, and to the Deputy Speaker, and to the deputy chairman of committees. For her thoughtful speech in moving this motion, and for her skilful presentation, I would like to say a word of congratulation to the member from Northumberland (Miss Jewett) as well as to the member from Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) for his able speech of seconding.
The riding of York South is marked by many things, but none more intriguing than the list of those who have been defeated for election to this house. I speak from experience. A right hon. gentleman, twice prime minister of this country and leader of his party, made his last stand for public office here. Brilliant parliamentarian, centre of many a national storm, Mr. Arthur Meighen did not pass the testing ground of York South. The victor of that day was to meet defeat, when the much beloved Mr. Joseph Noseworthy came, left and came again to this house. With a record over many years, Mr. William Beech has given much service and matched his two wins now with two losses. My immediate predecessor, my friend, Mr. David Lewis, a leading trade union lawyer, made his mark as a debater in this house and now adds York South to his losses. This is one of the anomalies of the party system. Elected, but never defeated, the Hon. J. Earl Lawson served as minister of national revenue.

And now that the subamendment and the amendment to this motion have been lost, redistribution, as mentioned in the speech from the throne, will probably see a rearrangement of this constituency, which runs from Oriole parkway at its easternmost tip to Jane street on the west. Its 63,000 voters represent an important cross section of achievement, not only in the two municipalities but in the wider metropolitan Toronto, in the affairs of the province of Ontario and in many things across this broad country. In government, industry, commerce, trade unionism, banking, the professions, the arts and education, the people of York South are well represented.
This electoral district consists of the village of Forest Hill and most of the township of York. At one time the township included the area between Scarborough and the Humber river. To attend a council meeting involved almost an entire day of travel. The fragmenting of this area into a series of municipalities has helped create the problems of metropolitan administration. The present township within the boundaries of York South is largely residential, while the main roadways afford extensive retail shopping facilities. Some important industries are located along its northern fringe. The village of Forest Hill constitutes about one fifth of the riding, and has been carefully planned to maintain its special character for residential living. It is well known for the high standard of its public educational system.
This government has given notice that it will introduce a number of important bills with a view to increasing the rate of economic growth. In order to achieve this result we must deliberately plan to reach ascending economic plateaus. Forward economic planning of such comprehensive proportions can only be the responsibility of government.
In the past we have lived with certain national illusions. For one, it was assumed that no matter who was in power we would automatically receive good government. With the ins or outs the prospects were equally good, it was said. The future of Canada was assured no matter how well we did our part. This optimistic illusion is now exposed. We must work hard with wisdom, patience, courage and imagination, to meet the many problems which confront us and assure for Canada days of more fruitful prospects and better realization. Economic myths have been no less embedded in our national being. Somehow we would always achieve that rate of growth which would take care of our many problems. A passionate controversy over responsibility for monetary and fiscal policy destroyed one illusion in recent years that bewitched those charged with high office.
The Address-Mr. Gelber
At the heart of our economic problem is the rate of capital investment, and the speech from the throne lists measures which show that this government will accept, as it should, responsibility for ensuring a sufficient flow of investment to maintain an adequate rate of growth. But the private sector remains the largest, and in some ways the most important area of investment. I was interested in the criteria outlined by the hon. member from Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) in this house the other day. I agreed with him as far as he went, but has he not oversimplified the problem? Our objectives must certainly be towards full employment and towards a higher standard of living for our people. But these two do not necessarily go together. In order to achieve both, we must improve and develop the productive capacity of this country through more efficient plant capacity and we must increase the capability of our labour force by investing in those skills that a developing economy will require. We must be particularly mindful of all these things since we, more than others, work in an open economy. The rate of growth here is intimately and directly associated with our international trading relationships. It seems to me that we must add to the criteria of the hon. gentleman in formulating an economic program for Canada.
To ensure a sufficient rate of growth we must maintain a climate of investment congenial to those whose capital commitment is necessary. This cannot be based on caprice or on short-run objectives. The investor has his choices, and we must so provide a framework of profitability and confidence that we attract an adequate flow of capital. But we are much concerned not only about the quantum of investment, but also about its quality. We must offer greater inducements for greater productivity. We want an adequate rate of growth, but not a lopsided one. The problem of inflation must also continue to be of concern.
In the over-all planning for Canadian economic expansion the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will be watched with special interest. The remarkable recovery of western Europe underscores both the importance of planning and the agreeable acceptance by the private investment sector of reasonable goals set out in a national program. The success of the European common market has set up special problems for Canada. A strong and prosperous western Europe is certainly a Canadian interest. I was particularly interested in the statement made in this house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) upon his return from the commonwealth meetings and those of GATT. The possible polarization of trade in the

The Address-Mr. Gelber Atlantic community around separate European and American axes would set up a threat to the leadership which the west must give to the whole tree world. The proposals of the Kennedy administration which are aimed at turning the European common market outwards are of great concern to us here.
Historically we have sought in European markets, principally British, to build a sufficient surplus of payments to meet our deficit with the United States. What happens to the other two sides of this triangle is vital to us. We must seek a place in the accommodations which are made. Certainly our present imbalance cannot persist. It is our labour which is being discriminated against, because the more we process our materials the greater are the obstacles of the U.S. tariff. Will the new patterns of trade be adequate to our needs? Will they provide avenues for the emerging states of Asia and Africa? The struggle for Atlantic trade patterns is also a political struggle and much of what we have taken for granted in our relations with our allies will have to be examined critically. There are new challenges, new issues, new opportunities for statesmanship and this government is particularly rich in the needed skills and endowments.
In the ceaseless search for world peace, Canada must maintain the friendliest association with her allies and must maintain the most cordial relations with all nations which seek to secure the international rule of law. This has not always been so. We particularly prize our association through the commonwealth with new states, which give us special approaches in Asia and Africa. Support for the United Nations is the touchstone of our foreign policy, and we give what aid we can to settle international differences by conciliation. Our diplomats are in the forefront of this struggle for peace and understanding.
In a world where starvation is the primary fact of life for more than half the human race, we cannot be unmindful of the needs of underdeveloped countries. We can assist them to solve their problems, and we have contributed to all the multilateral programs of the United Nations. Our major effort has been through the Colombo plan, and it seems to me that such bilateral programs provide the basis on which Canada's international economic assistance plans can be most readily increased. The argument is often made that defence appropriations impoverish foreign aid in competition for the national dollar. This view is too easily spoken and the problem not examined sufficiently closely. There is much that we can do within the existing economic context. A most likely field is in

the export of know-how. The new nations are most deficient in technical skills, and this aspect of assistance can be expanded if we offer reasonable inducements to Canadians who might be prepared to make careers in this new field of foreign service.
Addressing the international law association at McGill University some years ago, Mr. Dag Hammarskjold suggested that the United Nations should establish a corps of international civil servants. Men and women prepared to serve the underdeveloped countries would have the security and the career prospects which such a corps could offer with the support of the contributing national governments.
International careers are not opening up; they are becoming more restricted for Canadians. With the increase in membership at the United Nations, which we welcome, the number of jobs available to Canadians is becoming less and less. By opening this additional avenue the United Nations itself can become the vehicle for a full career of international service.
In lieu of this forward looking action by the United Nations, Canada might consider providing within its civil service specially recruited and specially trained people who would be available for posting abroad on attachment to governments needing their assistance and where such aid has been specifically requested. A portion of the cost must be paid by the recipient countries in counterpart funds. The great record of the Indian civil service and similar administrative agencies suggests that a role, now sought by newly independent governments, could be provided for Canadians to serve as others have served with great distinction, people proud in their traditions but modest in administrative and technical skills.
Our commitment to NATO is our most binding international engagement. As a signatory of the NATO pact we were undertaking to play a role in the affairs of Europe in peacetime which in two world wars we had shown to be our national interest. But Europe itself has not stood still. The entente between France and West Germany, which would have been considered impossible earlier, provides opportunities for new co-operation. The coal and steel community foreshadowed a successful trading association with Italy, France and West Germany together with the Benelux countries. This poses a problem for Britain and for those like Canada who have an important stake in British trading prospects.
The rebuff to Britain administered by France is of wider import than trade bargaining. It is political, and political in the most

serious meaning of that term. Nuclear power, not agriculture, is the issue.
Events are moving swiftly and we must be continually examining and re-examining our relationships. American nuclear supremacy is almost too easy an answer for giving military strength to NATO. Britain's special relationship to the United States, particularly in matters of nuclear policy, makes her specially suspect to General de Gaulle. When he says Britain is not sufficiently mature he means she is specially favoured.
NATO is tested by the struggle to establish three centres of nuclear power and nuclear technology within the alliance. The decentralization of control over some of the elements does not satisfy the demands with regard to the command problems of the alliance. German participation raises special anxieties.
Just as NATO itself intimately associated Canada with the defence of Europe, the new struggle is opening the door to an even more closely knit political relationship of Canada to western Europe. A new Europe has emerged and we must ensure that it unites us and does not set us apart. We may look to wider Atlantic horizons to find in some larger constellation a solution to our problems which arise in part from the very success of our efforts. In this developing Atlantic community we may yet look to resolve some of our present problems of trade and defence. But this does not diminish our concern for our wider trade relationships and our support for the United Nations. The struggle for disarmament as well must be persistent and be pursued with wisdom, tenacity and great patience. The stakes are the highest and our best efforts must be engaged.
Canada is moving because we choose to move. But the world about us is moving even more quickly. The optimistic, the automatic, the easy roles were illusory in any case, and we have been carried forward in a bound of good fortune. We have to assess our position critically and wisely. We have to conserve our forces of strength, of which national harmony and economic prosperity are among the most important. In association with our friends and allies we must seek without pause to resolve these problems of the greatest perplexity to advance the interests of Canada and of all mankind.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Speaker, Deputy Speaker and deputy chairman of committees on their election to their high offices. In congratulating the Speaker may I say that I was indeed very pleased that he was the one who received the call. In his 28902-5-25
The Address-Mr. Rapp previous experience as chairman of the public accounts committee, of which I had the honour to be a member, I know that he did a magnificent and impartial job. I should also like to congratulate the mover (Miss Jewett) and seconder (Mr. Choquette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I wish them well, with but one reservation, only during this parliament.
In taking part in the debate on the speech from the throne I should like to say from the outset that it is not my intention today to speak so much on what was mentioned in the speech from the throne but rather on what was not mentioned, and in particular a matter that received such great publicity during the election campaign. I refer to the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag.
As a preliminary I should like to say that at times I feel I should be the last man in the house to speak on a Canadian flag or, more specifically, on the red ensign. To me a flag is not just a piece of cloth on a pole. To my mind it is a symbol of what the country stands for.
I may be the only one in this house who has had the misfortune to live under more than one flag and I also realize I may be the only one here who has ever had to live under the flag of the hammer and sickle. I recall one sunny day in November, 1929, when I looked for the last time on that flag and, as is always the case when one comes to the end of a road or a span in life comes to a close, all the past appeared before me. All the things that happened under that flag, the revolution, one of the bloodiest in human history, all unfolded before my eyes. Under that flag there was to be built a community where democracy was supposed to be restored, where freedom, liberty and, above all, equality, would be given to all the people of that country.
I lived through those times but I also lived to see later times when millions sought to flee from this so-called democracy. I also lived to see the time when under that flag the revolution subsided and the so-called newly restored freedom, liberty and equality turned out to be farther from the grasp of the people than ever before. I also lived to see the day when under that flag dictatorship reached the highest point of despotism ever experienced anywhere in the world.
Human rights and freedom disappeared under that, flag while, at the same time, millions of lives were sacrificed to uphold the flag and all it stood for. As a result of this revolution millions of people looked for refuge under other flags in other countries such as Canada, and other freedom loving countries in the world.

The Address-Mr. Rapp
I was one of the more fortunate ones who succeeded in emigrating to another country, in my case to Canada, and I well recall stepping on Canadian soil and being able to see for the first time the Canadian flag which stood for principles quite contrary to those experienced under the flag of the hammer and sickle. I was also aware of the fact that under this Canadian flag thousands of Canadians had fought and given their lives to preserve freedom and democracy as we know them today, all symbolized in the Canadian flag.
The question arose in my mind: Will we now as new citizens achieve our desire for freedom and the democratic rights which are so dear to our hearts? Will we be allowed to become Canadian citizens? After 34 years in Canada I must say, Mr. Speaker, that Canada has lived up to all our expectations. I will always be grateful to this country for what it has done for me and my family. Canada has earned high respect and esteem throughout the world under this Canadian flag. Canada is a country to which many would like to come if they were only allowed to do so.
An incident which I will never forget happened only a couple of years after we came to Canada. This was the time when our first child had to attend school. Coming from a country where the schools not only served the purpose of education but also served the ends of indoctrination with the communist idea, it was a great satisfaction to us to see the union jack flying over our country school. I knew then and there that this was not going to be a place where our children would be indoctrinated with the ideologies of communism, fascism, or nazism. I can only speak with the highest regard and esteem of the Canadian educational system. It is available to all who have the ability, the will and some means. It was available to my family in abundance.
When we hear so much about the free education the people of the communist countries are supposed to enjoy, I often wonder if people are aware of the other side of the coin. I refer to the fact that you are nothing more or less than a tool of the state, and after the state has given you your education, it takes possession of you. This is not the case in Canada, as everybody knows. When the question comes up concerning a new distinctive Canadian flag, I will always recall the first time I looked upon the union jack and realized the things for which it stood. Latterly, of course, the red ensign, which was adopted on September 5, 1945, stood for all these things.
I am not the only one who is concerned with this issue of the flag. Many new Canadians will also be concerned with the question

of a new, distinctive Canadian flag, since all of them at one time or another lived under another flag. Undoubtedly the question will arise in their minds as to whether this new flag will be one which will stand for the same high principles, the same rights and privileges that have been afforded to Canadians of whatever race, creed or colour, as those which were available under the old flag, a flag under which Canada grew to the position of high esteem in which she is held by all the countries of the world. As a result of this national issue before us, all Canadians will search their hearts and souls in an attempt to find the right answer to the question of whether or not Canada should have a distinctive Canadian flag or retain the red ensign. An answer must be found and a decision must be made.
As I said at the outset, perhaps I should have been the last man to speak about the Canadian flag. My purpose in speaking, however, is only to enumerate the high principles for which Canada stands now, and for which she stood in the past, all symbolized in our Canadian flag. However, should the time ever come when this house decides to adopt a new Canadian flag then, as one who believes in democratic majority rule I would accept this decision and swear my loyalty to Canada under this new, distinctive Canadian flag of whatever design. At the same time, however, I should like to be around when the old flag, the red ensign, which to me is the free flag, is lowered for the last time. I should like to pay my last tribute to it, to touch it for the last time and then wipe away a tear or two because of my affection for the old Canadian flag, the only free flag I ever knew in my life and the flag by which Canada is known all over the world.

Mr. Speaker, allow me to congratulate you on the occasion of your appointment and to deliver my speech as if the Speaker himself were in the chair, because that is how it was prepared.
I am pleased to join with all those who have spoken before me in this debate to offer you the habitual congratulations upon your appointment to the office of Speaker of the House of Commons. I do so with pleasure and sincerity, the more so as I have had the privilege of knowing you outside the house and of appreciating your qualities of heart and mind.
I do not intend to compete with Demosthenes, in a flight of oratory, first because I would be hard put to do it and then because I see no point to it.
The debate on the speech from the throne will soon reach its eighth day and I doubt

that the administration of the affairs of the country, which has been entrusted to us, is further advanced than on the second day. I shall therefore refrain from giving my cooperation to this chronic standstill which paralyses us lawmakers. I know that one must suffer great pains to give birth to great ideas but heroism must not be extended to the point where one gets to be fond of those pains.
I could spend much time analysing the speech from the throne to bring out its flaws for the delight of the opposition and the confusion of government members, but previous speakers have done it for me during the first days, and I think that the government has suffered enough while the opposition has rejoiced enough.
I could also speak in praise of my con-situency and of my political heroes, but the Sherbrooke riding cannot be described; you have to know it to appreciate it and I heartily invite all hon. members of this house and their friends to come to see us. The tourist industry in my region would be thankful forever.
As for my heroes, I will not even mention their names because you would not accept them and it might make some people laugh.
To make sure that this brief contribution on my part does not sink into negativism, I should like to repeat a suggestion I made in the last parliament to the effect that this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne should be made shorter. My first thought would be to do completely away with the whole debate following that speech since the same topics have to come up again in our discussions on bills. But I think such a change would be too drastic, because we must provide some opportunities for politicians to show off their talents.
But so as not to break away from traditions too abruptly, I feel sure that we could set a maximum of three or four spokesmen for each party represented in this house and no one would suffer from that, certainly not our electors. Those speeches could take the form of a legal debate and the speakers taking part after the leaders would discuss only new developments instead of going back over the same stories all the time.
That way, Mr. Speaker, I am sure this debate would have come to an end several days ago and we would now be discussing legislation instead of just quibbling.
I thank you for bearing with me, and I apologize to the hon. members for monopolizing such precious minutes.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few hundred words to the many thousands which have been spoken on the subject of bilingualism and biculturalism. I am not sure that the term biculturalism has been defined in precise terms as it relates to Canada today, but I think it means that the French speaking citizens of Canada demand that the French fact be recognized in Canada, as it is in the province of Quebec at the present time, and to a limited extent throughout the federal legislature, federal courts and civil service.
It is stated in the speech from the throne that the government will foster the spirit of co-operative federalism. I believe that term "co-operative federalism" was publicly used for the first time at the founding convention of the New Democratic party in 1961. Both the program and the constitution of our party recognize the bicultural and bilingual character of all Canada. I do not think this recognition in our party program and constitution is

The Address-Mr. Prittie the result of the wisdom and foresight of the English speaking delegates to that founding convention. Rather, as I recall it, it was the Quebec delegation which forced the issue, and I remember one Ontario delegate remarking, when the matter came up for voting, "What the devil; let us vote for it if it makes them happy". I think that remark typifies the thinking of many English speaking Canadians. They bear no ill towards French Canadians. Quite the contrary; but they wonder what the fuss is all about. They simply do not understand why French Canada is angry at the present time, but the discussion which has been taking place during the past year has helped to inform them on the subject.
I suggest that to condemn all English speaking Canadians for the dissatisfaction of Quebec and the French speaking residents of other provinces, is a mistake. The average English speaking Canadian who lives in Halifax, Toronto, Brandon, Calgary or Vancouver is not responsible for whatever economic exploitation there has been in Quebec. He did not write the British North America Act. He is not responsible for the composition of the federal civil service, so do not blame him for all these things.
It may have been necessary on the part of the people of Quebec to overstate the case in order to be heard, but I think they have now achieved a result in that the rest of Canada is listening. I suggest the average English speaking Canadian is willing to listen, and he will listen much more readily to those who speak in moderate terms than to those who speak in extreme terms on this subject. It seems to me it serves no useful purpose to speak of ultimatums, a last chance for confederation or even, as the premier of Quebec did, of the state of Quebec.
I may say quite frankly I am critical of the press, but in this particular case I think they have done a fairly good job in recent months in reporting this subject. In my own area the Vancouver Sun sent one of its editorial writers to Quebec, and he has written a good series of articles on this subject, trying to explain to readers away out on the Pacific coast just what is the root of the controversy. Having said that, I can state the New Democratic party endorses the proposed royal commission on biculturalism.
More than that we agree there should be a reconsideration of the tax sharing agreements between the federal government and the provincial governments, but here I would add a word of caution and say that, while we believe the provinces do need sufficient revenues to carry out their proper functions of government, we do not want this carried to the extent that the federal government will be seriously weakened, because it too has very

serious and heavy responsibilities. We will also want to see the continuation of the equalization formula which has been in existence for a number of years.
If we are to remain a united country, and not just a collection of almost-autonomous provinces, it is essential that some of the revenues collected in the richer provinces be distributed to some of those provinces which have less than an average income. There has to be a great deal of compromise on this question of the allocation of revenues.
Mr. Speaker, while we endorse the proposed royal commission and believe it can serve a very useful purpose, we think there are a number of steps which could be immediately taken by the federal government without waiting for the report of the commission, particularly in the case of bilingualism. I should like to make a few personal comments on that point. None of us expect that Canada will be completely bilingual at any time. Far from it; but we want it to be more bilingual than it is now. In most cases this means that the efficient teaching of French should be encouraged, and we feel more use could be made of instruments now available to serve this purpose.
For example, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has done quite a good job in this field in a rather limited way, and I imagine the reason was that it was limited by funds. I refer particularly to the series of programs carried for the last several years under the direction of Professor Vinay of the University of Montreal, the series called "Speaking French." It is an excellent form of instruction and I would like to see more of it both on C.B.C. television and radio.
I would also like to see some C.B.C. French outlets in parts of Canada which are not now served by the French network. Last year I made a plea for a French language outlet on the lower mainland of B.C. I suggested a low power relay station, a relatively inexpensive type of installation. In the lower mainland of B.C. there are approximately 50,000 people of French speaking origin, some of them Canadians, and some who come from France, Belgium and Switzerland, but at the present time they have no radio service in the French language. The establishment of low power relay stations in several parts of the country could carry the French network to places where it is not now heard. This is something which could be done without waiting for a royal commission. It just requires the allocation of funds to the C.B.C. and then it can do the job.
As one who has been on both the receiving and the giving end of language instruction in Canadian schools I know just how bad

38S
and tedious it has been. In past years students in the English speaking provinces have had to suffer through a great many French lessons that were very dull and overly bookish, but there are now available modern techniques which can make language instruction much more efficient and interesting. I refer in particular to the installation of language laboratories in schools. They can do this kind of job much better than it has ever been done in the past, and this is one type of federal assistance to education which might be quite acceptable. Special funds might be made available to the various departments of education, which in turn could allocate them to school boards for the installation of language laboratories, not only for the teaching of French where that is necessary but also for the teaching of English in parts of the province of Quebec. This is a practical measure and I know that many school boards would like to do it, but they hesitate because the cost of these laboratories is quite high.
Apart from the measures which the federal government can take on its own to promote bilingualism and biculturalism in Canada there are certain actions which can only be taken by the provinces, particularly in the field of education. I understand that one of the demands of French Canada is that instruction in the French language be available in provinces other than Quebec. Personally I agree that this should be done wherever there is a sizeable group of people to receive this instruction. But I would suggest to those who are advocating this step that they be patient and prepared to go slow on it. It is one for which they will have to wait, I think, until public opinion in the provinces changes somewhat. Even in the province of Ontario I noticed last fall a sharp reaction, I believe it was in Scarborough, when demands were made to the separate school board-a board which one would think would be quite sympathetic-for more bilingual instruction. I think this will come, but its advocates should be prepared to be rather patient. Finally, Mr. Speaker, on this particular topic of bilingualism and biculturalism I think the point has been made and English speaking Canada is now becoming aware of the problem. They want to see an improvement, but there are those who think as I do-and I think my views are shared by many in English speaking Canada-in wishing to retain Canada as a unified country. We do not want a collection of, as I said, almost autonomous states in a very loose confederation. I think we can achieve a more bicultural nation and still retain a strong Canada.
I was rather disappointed that there was no mention in the speech from the throne of
The Address-Mr. Prittie aid in education, and particularly for universities in Canada. This subject has come to the fore in the last day or so while the Canadian universities federation have been in Ottawa presenting a brief to the Prime Minister. They have asked for federal grants of $300 million in the next three years. These grants amount to a great deal of money. I know that the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches are besieged with requests for help, all of which call for the spending of money, but some things are more important than others. Certainly the financing of university education is one of the most important considerations at the present time. The funds available through the Canada Council in the form of university capital grants are certainly not sufficient. There was only $50 million to begin with and that sum has been considerably reduced. I think this is a matter upon which the federal government will have to take a stand very soon. They do pay certain operating costs, but what is required are capital grants for the construction of new colleges and universities.
I have a general and a particular interest in this topic. My particular interest arises because it was announced recently that a new university, to be called the Simon Fraser university, would be built in Burnaby, specifically in Burnaby-Coquitlam. This university will be on a magnificent site. It will be the third provincial university in British Columbia, and it will be a very expensive undertaking. The provincial government will have to do their part. I would agree right away that the present government of British Columbia does not do the part it should in the financing of universities. I hope we can expect more help from them. Certainly, unfortunately, the students will have to meet part of the cost, but if the university is to be built, federal assistance will be necessary. We do not ask for any special consideration but we hope we may share increased support in the form of capital grants for all universities.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I noted with pleasure that in the speech from the throne there was reference to the establishment of a municipal development and loan board. This has long been advocated. It was advocated by members of this party as far back as the early 1950's and possibly before that. However, we are not concerned with who advocated it but we are very pleased that something is to be done about it. As one who spent several years in municipal life on a municipal council I can appreciate the problems facing people in local government trying to meet the costs of urban expansion. Therefore I shall look with great interest at the detailed legislation on this particular topic. There were a number of

The Address-Mrs. Konantz other proposals in the speech from the throne which I think show promise but with regard to which we must await the detailed legislation in order to pass final judgment upon them.

Mr. Speaker, as a new member of this house I have been sitting here for eight days listening to other hon. members telling about their constituencies. Most of these constituencies have been either in Ontario, Quebec, the maritimes or British Columbia. For this reason I thought it was my duty to let hon. members know about the area I come from, Winnipeg South, Manitoba.
First, sir, through you I would like to congratulate the Speaker on his appointment. I know, from what I have heard in these last eight days, that he will always show great fairness and clear judgment in all our debates. We are indeed fortunate to have you, sir, as our Deputy Speaker, as we are the deputy chairman of committees. The appointments have been excellent. I would like to take this opportunity of thanking the hon. member from Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) for the very kind things he said about me in this house earlier this afternoon. I only hope I can live up to his expectations. I want to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As I listened to the hon. member from Northumberland (Miss Jewett) I was reminded that I, too, had connections in her constituency for, sir, my great grandmother first settled there when she came from Scotland. She and her husband had been given a beautiful farm by her father. Then, too, I thought of my grandmother who, as a bride leaving a lovely part of Ontario, travelled across lakes and up rivers by canoe with her husband, a Hudson's Bay factor, to Norway House which is situated at the most northerly end of lake Winnipeg. I have her diary, and in it she describes the skill of the Indians as they handled their cargoes through the rapids and over the portages into this rugged territory. Those were truly pioneering days.
Mr. Speaker, there are only two of us with the government to represent Manitoba. I must admit we Liberals had hoped during the campaign that there would be more and I can assure you there will be after the next election. However, I can guarantee that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) and I will do our best to hold the fort, so to speak. And I believe we shall be capable of doing this, for I must remind you, sir, that the minister is a descendant of a great man who held the territory which is now Manitoba for Canada back in the years of 1869 and 1870, while I myself, as a descendant of the first
[Mr. Prittie.l
governor of the Hudson's Bay Company, a man who developed the tremendous area of Rupert's Land, feel that my roots go deep. Our pride in our ancestors has made us both determined, and we will always fight to a finish. It seems extraordinary that we two, coming from such a background, should be representing the territory where years ago French and English stood side by side to defend Fort Garry and the little community across the Red river against the penetration of the fur traders from the south. Today we two, French and English, stand together to work for our people. I am sure my hon. friend and I will prove to other hon. members that French and English can work together with great harmony and understanding.
My constituency of Winnipeg South is a large one in which 114,000 people live. It is primarily an urban area. It might be interesting to hon. members to know that in this one federal constituency there are five provincial ridings. All these provincial seats are held by Conservative members of our Manitoba government; three are cabinet ministers-our attorney general, our minister of trade and commerce and the minister of labour. I can assure you, sir, that it took all my courage, a woman, to go into this territory to try to win this seat for the Liberal party. It was achieved only because of the magnificent job that was done by over 2,000 workers under the excellent guidance of a brilliant campaign committee. Here, I must pay tribute to my opponent Mr. Gordon Chown who was the hon. member for Winnipeg South for the last two sessions and deputy speaker of this house last year. My family and his family have been friends for many, many years. It was indeed unfortunate that the two of us should be candidates in this constituency of Winnipeg South, but then I was trying with my people to take this seat once again for the Liberals. I have been told that Mr. Chown through the years gave excellent service to his party. I know he was very well liked in this house, and that he will be missed by his many friends.
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to say much about my constituency but I do wish to say a little about the people I represent. Their ancestors came first out of ships from Hudson's Bay, then by the long river route of the fur traders and as Selkirk settlers. These people knew the hardships of frontier life-wars between fur traders, floods on the Red river, massacres, cold, hunger, loneliness. Being so isolated they developed their own ways of life, their own thoughts, their own independence.
With the C.P.R. railroad reaching this frontier town of Winnipeg in 1881 came the

great surge of settlement. People from all over Europe brought their skills, their culture, their experience. These people were so far away from any other centre in Canada they were forced to make their own amusement, develop their own interests in music, dramatics, art.
The growing of grain brought the first wealth to this part of Canada and I believe that this made everyone very conscious about business in other countries. World wide interests were developed, so today you find among the people of my constituency the fierce energy of the pioneer, a kind of informality that was first found at our early forts, a gaiety that has come down through the years, a people with a forward look, and with a world wide feeling. I am proud to represent these people. I am not bilingual, but 1 found that as I went around the constituency during this last campaign, I was able to meet new friends in three languages- but with an appalling accent-simply by saying "bonjour", "au revoir", "buon giorno", "arrivederci", "slava esusu khristu".
I can assure hon. members that the people of south Winnipeg will welcome the proposals set out in the speech from the throne. They will be particularly interested in the municipal development and loan board which is to finance municipal works projects; in the Canada development corporation which will channel savings into industrial growth, and in the economic council to be set up to develop more employment and more efficient production. In addition, they will be interested in the proposal to set up a new department of industry because, like so many other parts of Canada we, too, have suffered from the ills and causes of unemployment.
The people of Winnipeg South will welcome the proposed amendments to the National Housing Act and the setting up of a national contributory pension plan. The establishment of a commission for the redistribution of commons seats will definitely affect Winnipeg South, for here it takes three to four city votes to equal one rural vote. As one who was thrown into an election campaign without any political experience I welcome the review of the Canada Elections Act which is foreshadowed. We of the west are a practical people and I believe our elections are too expensive and the campaigns too long. They try the patience of the voter, and in my opinion our election machinery could be modernized.
The setting up of a new committee on parliamentary procedure is an excellent course to follow. This committee would, I realize, be one of many which have been named in the past but I would like to think that our present members will be strong enough to
The Address-Mrs. Konantz see that the findings will be put into effect. Surely the time has come when the business of this house can be streamlined.
A study of biculturalism by a federal-provincial commission set up for that purpose is obviously needed. All French Canadians should feel at home anywhere in Canada.
Plans for the Canadian centennial celebration will give every Canadian a chance to work together for projects that will have real and lasting value. I urge our government to give the leadership that has been so badly needed at the federal level during these last two years.
There is one problem which concerns not only my own constituency but constituencies all over Manitoba, and I feel I should draw it to the attention of all hon. members.
That is the proposed move of the Trans-Canada Air Lines maintenance and overhaul base from Winnipeg to Dorval. There is a long history behind this proposal, and it would seem that through the last five years the government and T.C.A. while saying one thing did another. I do not intend to discuss the details here but I urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) and his department to delve into every angle of this problem before any decisions are made. One thousand of our most highly skilled craftsmen and mechanics and their families would be involved in such a move. Did anyone in the previous government think twice of how such a move would affect these people? It would involve the giving up of their homes, their environment with their friends and relatives they know so well, uprooting their children in the midst of their education, transferring them all into an area so different in every way to what they have known. Surely these people must be given some consideration. T.C.A. is recognized as a good air line but it does not operate on the same terms as a privately-owned venture. It is government-owned and supported by public funds. Surely the federal government should have a definite say in its policies. The Minister of Transport knows that there will be a delegation to protest once again, with representation from our provincial government, the municipalities, business and industry and the trade unions and workers, indeed I could say our whole community. I am confident that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will carry out the pledge he made to the Liberal candidate for Winnipeg South Centre during the election campaign, that "a new Liberal government will immediately clarify the position of T.C.A. in the light of the full facts which up to now the government has obscured or suppressed."
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) for the statement he made before this house

The Address-Mrs. Konantz last Friday on the two meetings that he attended in London and Geneva. I was particularly interested in what he had to say about expansion of trade to developing countries. You may not know, sir, but I have been closely associated with the United Nations association in Canada for the last seven years. In order to learn more about the work of the United Nations beyond the general assembly I have had the privilege of being able to travel, first through the Asia region of the children's fund under the auspices of UNICEF. This took me to Japan, Formosa, Hong Kong, the Phillipines, Thailand, Cambodia, India and Pakistan. I continued on from there and made brief visits in Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel. A few years later, with the co-operation of my friends at the United Nations, I travelled for three months through nine countries in Africa, Ghana, Nigeria, South Africa, Rhodesia, Tanganyika, Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia and the United Arab Republic. Quite frankly, it was the result of these two intensive trips that made me decide to enter politics. Between the years 1956 and 1961 I had found that our image abroad had deteriorated to such an extent that I was anxious to do anything that I could to serve my country. This was the time that we needed the leadership of our great Canadian, one who has given this country such service, who is known so well in so many world capitals for his outstanding ability in international affairs. I speak, of course, of the Prime Minister, a man who is so highly regarded at the United Nations, indeed all around the world. He is a man of peace and understanding, a man who already during his short term of office as Prime Minister has brought credit to our country by visiting both Britain and the United States to cement old friendships. I am proud to be associated with a friend that I have known for many years.
There is not time here today for me to go into the many questions relating to foreign aid. However, I want to say I am one of those Canadians who believes that Canada is not giving enough money, enough technical assistance or enough leadership. But I am one of those people who believes that foreign aid must be carefully planned, co-ordinated with other nations and followed through so that the main objectives can be achieved. I have seen the value of the simple community development schemes in the villages of central Africa. I was told that the women of the Masai tribe could never be trained. But I will never forget the day that I saw these women doing a feeding project for the children of their greatest enemy, the Kikuyu, who were starving as a result of the drought.


Again I was privileged to witness the opening of an aluminum plant in Lagos, Nigeria, financing of which had been arranged for between Britain, Canada and Nigeria. After watching the way cargoes were taken from the great ships off the coast of Ghana by outrigger canoes, I understood so well the need for the great new harbour at Tema. Foreign aid is not charity. It is more than good business, it represents a true partnership with those less fortunate nations of the world whose living standards must be raised if the free world is to bring a better life for everyone. I pay tribute, Mr. Speaker, to the Canadian students who have gone to Africa and Asia under the auspices of the Canadian university services overseas. These young people are serving our country and learning at the same time, and I am sure that what the sponsor of this program had to say is true, that when these young people come back from a year or two of living and working in these countries they will be far more valuable citizens at home.
It would seem, sir, that there never was a time when there must be greater understanding between young and old, between all our people, between communities and provinces and well beyond our Canadian shores-an understanding between nations. I pray that I will be worthy of the trust that the people of Winnipeg South have placed in me. (Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I should like at the outset to congratulate you on your new appointment. I should like also, through you, to congratulate the new Speaker of the house.
