Mr. Speaker, it is not easy, these days, to deal with Quebec and the French Canadians, and to explain what is going on in the province of Quebec.
I know that the bombings by the madmen of the F.L.Q. have spread confusion, but I should like to assure the house as well as all those who are listening that these bombings are the work of only a few who have been condemned by all the associations, by all the people of the province of Quebec endowed with a sound judgment, and even by the most fiery separatists.
There is surely a revolution boiling up in many fields right now in the province of Quebec, but it is a perfectly peaceful revolution, and it can be summed up this way.
The French Canadians want to play a greater part in the economy of the province of Quebec. Nobody can find any fault with that, it is a perfectly natural aspiration. It must even be encouraged by all possible means. There is unquestionably in the province of Quebec a movement, especially amongst the young people, according to which our young French Canadians should play a more active part in the economic, social and political life of the province.
To begin with, there has been changes in the field of education. Under the Hon. Paul Sauve, great steps were made in this field. Under the government led by Mr. Barrette, nine marking pieces of legislation were enacted, while since Mr. Lesage came into power, inquiry commissions have been set up and a real effort has been made in this direction.
There is something quite noticeable right now in the province of Quebec, in the streets or everywhere. When one talks with young people, they show a very real desire to learn, to qualify themselves, and this desire is sometimes reflected in outbursts of impatience.
I wish to point out to the house that this is a very invigorating atmosphere, and one that we shall not be able to destroy.
There has also been great changes in the church in Quebec; perhaps the church was somewhat too traditionalist. But today, there is an extreme liberalism boiling up in this same church. There is a modernism with which we were not familiar before. There is also a certain secularization taking place in the Catholic religion in the province of Quebec.
All this has contributed to create a new mentality among our people.
Unfortunately, that trend which reflects that great desire on the part of the French Canadians to play an even more important role in the province of Quebec gives rise 28902-5-26
The Address-Mr. Balcer along the way to a wave of separatism, a wave powerful enough to warrant our attention.
Two or three years ago, people did not take that separatist movement seriously and, for my part, I felt it was but another one of those short-lived movements which come up about every 20 years. I thought it was politically weak, that is weak in numbers and not homogeneous enough. But today, the movement has become more homogeneous and even turned into a political party.
I must tell you that it is quite strong among the youth of the province of Quebec. That even surprised me. I made a survey among the young people of my beautiful city of Three Rivers and was able to find that, not only among the university students, but also among those in our convents and colleges, that separatist feeling is real.
If we look for an example of that force, we simply have to notice the outbidding which is done at the provincial level towards the separatists. I can give further evidence of the seriousness of the situation. We just have to read the article under Peter Newman's byline which appeared last week in Maclean's magazine, which makes us wonder if, in fact, Mr. Lesage, the premier of Quebec, would not become Canada's prime minister or the president of the Quebec republic. I know that this article by Peter Newman contains a flash of wit but there is also quite a bit of seriousness.
Anyway, it is obvious that Quebec is going to sink more deeply into separatism.
As for me, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the only way we can provide for such an eventuality is to ensure that the young French Canadians who have a great desire to play their part in the economy and in the political life of the province of Quebec, be able to participate as well in the economic, political and social life of the whole of Canada.
And to do that, ladies and gentlemen-I beg your pardon, that was left over from the last election campaign-sacrifices will have to be made on both sides. Besides we are somewhat used to that because it must be remembered that, in the last hundred years, living as we do next door to the American giant, we have had to make sacrifices in order to keep our independence and our sovereignty. We have had to accept a standard of living lower than our southern neighbour's, only to be part of that sovereign Canada.

The Address-Mr. Balcer
If we want to keep our country whole and united, we will have to make still more sacrifices. There is no doubt that our English speaking friends in the other provinces, as well as in the province of Quebec, will also have to make sacrifices. Why? Because they have the upper hand in our country's business and especially in the central state.
The royal commission on biculturalism or bilingualism will undoubtedly do some good since it has been approved. However, it will take two years to present its report. And it is much too long considering the turmoil in which the province of Quebec finds itself at the present time.
Canadians must realize without delay that we, French Canadians, want a change as soon as possible. First of all, Canada must have a distinctive flag without further delay. Even though we urge French Canadians of the province of Quebec to believe in a great and united Canada and to be Canadians first of all and Quebeckers after, they always reply along the same lines: "How can we believe such a state of things, how can we have a national feeling strong enough to believe in a united Canada when we do not have a distinctive flag or a national anthem such as 'O Canada'?" I ask then all Canadians to sincerely weigh the arguments I have just outlined concerning this problem.
At this time, it would be appropriate to make an effort in the field of federal services. As you know, the old question remains to be dealt with. What French Canadians consider most insulting, is to see that they are not proportionately represented in the central administration.
French Canadians do not hold as many senior posts as they should. I think that the best way of rectifying the situation now is to grant to each bilingual person, that is to anybody who has taken the trouble to learn both this country's languages, a supplement of 5 per cent in every civil service examination.
I want to call the attention of the house to a particular point. I would like the cities of Ottawa and Hull to become an essentially bilingual federal district which would really represent the union of both cultures and of both ethnic groups in this country. First of all, there is the needed number of people. All that is required is to create a federal district comprising Hull and Ottawa under a commission where both ethnic groups would be represented in equal numbers. French Canadians from the province of Quebec will then really feel that this is their

country's true capital and will really feel at home here. Such a suggestion would, of course, require some sacrifice, and a great deal of consideration on the part of our English speaking friends.
However, 1 hope that they realize what the situation is at present in the province of Quebec, because it is really a rather difficult one.
Further, our Anglo-Saxon friends, mainly in the province of Quebec, could make true friends among French Canadians by helping to create the impression that the latter may live as successfully in our confederate system as English Canadians.
I now come to the industrial field. I know that some laudable efforts have been made in that direction. However, if we look around us, for instance in the beautiful town of Three Rivers, which, incidentally, besides being certainly the finest city in Canada is also the greatest paper manufacturing centre in the world, where paper is made from pulp-wood taken from crown lands in the district of Mauricia, and where five or six large paper mills have been operating for the last 40 years, we would see that, unfortunately, French Canadians working in those paper mills, who thoroughly know their trade, as they have been employed there all that time, seldom rise above the rank of foreman.
In the last few years, something has been done along these lines, but our effort should be increased. Of course, there are people who say: "Perhaps they did not have all the necessary education and technical preparation." However in that same period, at St. Jerome and Mont Rolland, a French Canadian firm set up a paper mill that was as successful as those in Three Rivers. So I think that in that field, big corporations will have to make sacrifices.
Indeed some people say that these big industries had the necessary capital for that purpose, but I feel that this argument is slightly exaggerated. In fact, I could mention the example of one company that came to Canada with a capital of $1.5 million at the very beginning of world war II; today it has a capital of more than $350 million, because it received financial help from the governments.
As a matter of fact, I am of the opinion that the argument put forward by the French Canadians: "We do not have capital" also has some flaws.
On the other hand French Canadians must be prepared for sacrifices and they must consent to make a serious effort to save and

strengthen confederation. We should not forget that confederation, which has been in existence for 100 years, constitutes a formula which has been of some service to the French Canadians, which enabled our group to develop, maybe not as fast as we would have liked to, but it nevertheless rendered immeasurable services. I am not one of those who pretend that we should destroy confederation, because it does not serve any purpose any longer. Confederation made Canada the great modern country it is today.
When French Canadians ask for changes, they should not forget that we have retained our ethnical individuality through confederation.
Let us remember that while we might feel we face serious problems today as far as saving confederation is concerned, those problems are very minute ones compared to the problems faced by Cartier and Macdonald in 1867.
This is why I believe that the ultimatum delivered by Mr. Lesage, the premier of the province of Quebec, was out of place. In my opinion, it was Mr. Lesage's duty to use that bit of common sense which would have been expected from the present leader of the province of Quebec. Quebec undoubtedly needs increased revenues and there are undoubtedly improvements to be made in the field of taxation, but did not our government increase equalization payments from 10 to 16 per cent in the short years we were in office? It would have been possible to discuss those problems around a conference table, and that is why I am asking the federal government to call a meeting of the representatives of the various provinces to discuss the problem of taxation.
I think everyone can expect Mr. Lesage to come to the conference table, as the representative for the province of Quebec, to get a better tax-sharing arrangement. That ultimatum of Mr. Lesage to the effect that the province of Quebec would get out of confederation if it did not get 25 per cent of taxes, should not have been delivered.
French Canadians have a right to make claims but their requests must retain a sense of measure. We must not forget that confederation was very beneficial to us and that it still is today.
I do not think that the statement made by the minister for municipal affairs, Mr. La-porte, to the effect that provinces had to be sovereign states united into a confederation, is likely to improve relations between the various provinces in Canada or between the two ethnic groups.
Nowadays, we see the European countries, age-long enemies, stand shoulder to shoulder to form the common market.

Mr. Speaker, I sincerely think that if we so wish Canada will live another hundred years as a great country. Sacrifices will have to be made on both sides and federal as well as provincial representatives of the people will have to show great statesmanship. We all want Canada to be a great country. We want both ethnic groups to be able to develop according to their aspirations. That can be done if we go hand in hand, shoulder to shoulder. I am certain that Canada will be a strong country, a great country and that a bright future lies before us.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether or not it is because I do not have on my skates, but it feels much more slippery here than it does on the ice. I should like to offer my congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker, and also to the Deputy Speaker on your election to these offices. I had occasion to get to know the Deputy Speaker a little bit during his first election campaign when I visited his constituency in order to help him in my own small way. I am certainly greatly pleased with the honour he has received in this appointment.
I should like also to congratulate the mover (Miss Jewett) and the seconder (Mr. Cho-quette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They certainly set a good example and I know that it is one with which I shall not be able to keep up; but I will certainly give it a good try. The position of the Speaker in this house reminds me a little bit of the referee in a hockey game. He has to know the rules of the house and he has to be able to set them out. Some Speakers are a little more rigid than others, and some are a little lenient. Sometimes they have-to hang on a misconduct penalty, as happened in the last parliament to one of the Social Credit members. As a matter of fact the Speaker had to call on the Sergeant-at-Arms to make sure the hon. member went to the penalty box, but I am confident that we will have a little better conduct in this parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I have been a little slow in rising to make my maiden speech. I was not sure whether I should speak right away or wait for a while, but I received so much publicity in the last parliament by not speaking that I could not hope to achieve that much again.
Speaking for the first time in the House of Commons is a rather awesome feeling for a new member. It is not like speaking before an ordinary crowd. We have hon. members who are reading their newspapers, some doing

The Address-Mr. Kelly their correspondence and others get up and leave just before one begins to speak. Then there is the odd one who is catching up on a little sleep that he missed. But seriously, sir, I would like to thank all hon. members of this and the previous house, and all the government staff who have been so kind in offering me their assistance. As a rookie in the house I was pretty green. I still am; but all the people I mentioned have been very kind to me and I would like to extend my thanks to them.
When it comes right down to it, the House of Commons reminds one of an amphitheatre in the days of the Romans when, having concluded your efforts, you look up to the gallery to see whether you get the thumbs up sign.
I first became acquainted with my riding of York West during my school days at St. Michael's College. I used to take the girls out from St. Joseph's and ride the streetcar down to the end of the line where we went dancing at the Old Mill. As a matter of fact we had to walk the last 500 yards or so because money was a little scarce in those days. Since then however the riding has changed greatly. It has become one of the fastest growing areas in the country.
It is bounded on the eastern side by the historic Humber river, on the south by lake Ontario, on the west by the new international airport and on the north by Thistletown and the Albion road. It is really a melting pot in a melting pot, and its population consists of pretty nearly every type of nationality conceivable. It has industries both large and small, approximately 800 in all. Some are Canadian owned and some are subsidiaries of United States firms.
One company in York West with a sales promotion of about $6,500,000 has just expanded into the United States, setting up a branch in Manhattan, New York, right in the heart of the American competition, but with no fear of not coming out on top. I think this is remarkable at a time when we are worried about how U.S. companies are taking over Canadian firms, and when we are worried about how Canadians will fare as we decrease tariffs on exports and imports. I feel this company deserves a great deal of credit. Also in York West we have a first in Canada, and that is pay T.V. I am happy about this, Mr. Speaker, because it gives me an opportunity to appear before my constituents every Sunday night.
As I have said, York West is one of the fastest growing areas in the country. Between the last two elections it showed an increase in eligible voters of approximately 6,000. My constituency is about 116 square miles in area

and holds 100,000 voters. I may say that to represent so many people is a big job.
Because it is a fast growing community we have an influx of many families with a lot of young children, and these children have to have an education. We are pretty proud of the educational system we have in York West, both academic and physical. Academic education comes under provincial jurisdiction, but the physical education is a concern of all Canada, and comes under both federal and provincial jurisdiction. I feel that in the past few years we have become rather lax in regard to our physical fitness, probably because of the many modem conveniences we have which we never had 50 or 60 years ago. It boils down to the fact that we do not get enough physical exercise, and I believe a physical fitness program should be carried out to the fullest possible degree. I might point out, sir, that we suffer from a lack of physical exercise in this house. The only exercise some hon. members get is rising to speak often, but that is not a well balanced program.
I have some comments to make with regard to a Canadian flag and a national anthem. I was raised by my father and mother to honour and respect the Queen and the flag, but I am one of the younger generation and maybe this is why I have some of the feelings I do. In my career I have had the opportunity of travelling a little bit around the world and of appearing before crowds in foreign countries. When my team appeared in public, before our performance we stood in the spotlight and they used to play "God Save the Queen." Of course we stood at attention and we were very proud to do so. But during the last few years "O Canada" has been played the odd time. As I have stood before these people in a foreign country and they started to play and sing "O Canada, our home and native land" I have felt great pride and my chest stood out a little more. They were singing about our land, our home.
All this made me feel we should have a flag and a national anthem. This Canada of ours is young. It is a young land. People are coming to it from many different countries to settle here and be Canadians, and we should have our own national anthem and a flag that is representative of all of Canada.

During the election campaign and after I was elected I was asked, as I imagine most members of parliament have been asked, why I decided to run as a member of parliament. I know this is the feeling of all hon. members. However, there was one reason in particular which I should like to mention. I had the opportunity of meeting our Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on several occasions and I admired and respected him a great deal. The more I talked to him, the more I read of his past political history, the more I thought this man could be the tonic Canada needs. I felt he could do a whale of a job for the future of Canada. That was one reason for my running as a member of parliament. Then after I had been in the house for a short time and had more occasion to be closer to him and see him at work, my respect and admiration grew. I think that this government, with its legislation put forward under the leadership of our Prime Minister, will put Canada where she should be.

Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to add my congratulations to those of previous speakers upon your appointment. I should also like to congratulate the Speaker of the house and the other officers upon their appointment. May I also congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I thought they made an excellent contribution to the debate. Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the hon. member for York West (Mr. Kelly) upon the very interesting speech he made this afternoon. If this is an augury of the speeches he will make in the future, introducing a little humour as he did today, I am sure we will all be very grateful.
As a representative of Simcoe East and a member of this parliament and of the previous Conservative regime I should like to say that
The Address-Mr. Rynard I am more than proud to be a Canadian. I am more than proud to have been a member of previous parliaments, when so much was achieved under a Conservative government.
I think it is well for us all to remember that this is a great country which has done great things. I do not think I can do better than quote from the Ottawa Journal of May 1, wherein appeared an article entitled "A house left in good order". I think that after the election all of us should be proud of the position we occupy and have attained as Canadians. This article in the Ottawa Journal says:
He left-
This is referring to Mr. Diefenbaker:
-a country whose national production in 1962 had climbed 8 per cent to a peak of $40.4 billion-
Mr. Speaker, that is the first time in the history of the western world that any country of less than 20 million people has achieved such a great increase in gross national product. The article continues:
He left him with a country which, after years of trade deficits, had at last achieved a favourable trade balance.
I think all of us, no matter what our political affiliations are, can be proud of the achievement Canada has made in this regard. The article then says:
He left him with a country which, on the testimony of President Kennedy, had achieved a greater price stability than any other western industrial nation.
He left him with a country whose reserves of gold and U.S. currency had been brought to $2,700,000,000-the greatest reached in years.
He left him with a country in which, during 1962, trade had reached an all-time high; in which manufacturing had jumped by 8 per cent, construction by 8.2 per cent, business capital investment by 4.8 per cent, outlays for new machinery and equipment by 8.6 per cent, and consumer spending by 5 per cent.
In short, Mr. Diefenbaker left Mr. Pearson with a country whose people were producing more, selling more, earning more and saving more than ever before in their history.
Mr. Speaker, I do not say this as a matter of politics, but as a Canadian I am proud of what has been achieved. The article continues:
Mr. Pearson has said that he will "get the economy going", "restore confidence".
If Mr. Pearson can "get the economy going" beyond an increase of 8 per cent in the gross national product in a single year, we shall all be grateful to him-
I for one, Mr. Speaker, hope that he can.
The article continues:
But what many must wonder about, in the light of the facts we have cited, is what Mr. Pearson can have in his mind when he talks of "restoring confidence". Was there really any lack of confidence, or reason for lack of confidence, in a

The Address-Mr. Rynard
country which in trade and income and price stability surpassed every other western nation in 1962?
Again, Mr. Speaker, I am proud to be a Canadian and a member oi this parliament:
We must all hope that Mr. Pearson does well; to wish him well is but to wish well for Canada. But for truth's sake, if for nothing else, let Mr. Pearson and his friends stop trying to give the impression that they took over a broken-down Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, there are a few points to which I wish to refer. During the last election, in the campaign promises and statements of the Liberal party were to be found items referring to early tax reforms, a balanced budget, municipal aid and many other things. I should first of all like to deal with the promise made to establish a municipal bank where this meets, of course, with provincial approval, from whom money could be borrowed at favourable rates on the advice of the province concerned. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the previous government had been doing this through the winter works program and by providing money at low rates of interest for the building of sewage plants, waterwork establishments, and so on. The municipalities were also given the incentive that if the work was completed in a certain length of time some of the debt was written off.
The municipal taxpayer is hard pressed at the moment by taxes that are needed to pay for local needs and I am surprised at the archaic way in which we are collecting money from taxpayers at the municipal level, then giving money back to the provinces, which is in turn given by the provinces to the municipalities in the form of grants. I would ask hon. members to consider the cost and the machinery involved in collecting this money at the federal level, giving it back to the provinces, going through all the machinery again and all the people necessary to handle it, then the provinces giving it back to the municipalities after the amount necessary for handling has been deducted.
Today in most municipalities 50 per cent or more of the tax dollar is spent on education. This is very necessary but it occurs to me that the federal government should be making larger grants to the provinces in this area. As we all know, they administer the Unemployment Insurance Act and are responsible for dealing with the effects of unemployment. We also know it has been found in surveys that the ranks of the unemployed are largely made up of those who are uneducated. It seems to me, therefore, that we should use our best efforts in educating people to a higher level, especially if
[Mr. Kynard.l
this will help ease the unemployment situation, as we know from these studies it will. It seems to me the federal government should be accepting a greater responsibility with regard to helping the municipalities meet their education costs. It occurs to me that the federal government did in effect accept this principle when it went across Canada building hundreds of technical schools and accepting 75 per cent of the cost. We should go on from there and help the municipalities cover their education needs.
The Canadian Tax Foundation has published a book called "The Burden of Canadian Taxation" by I. J. Goffman. It divides the people according to three levels of income -those earning less than $4,000, those earning between $4,000 and $7,000 and those earning over $7,000. It is estimated that more than $6 billion a year is collected as taxation by the three levels of government-this survey, by the way, was made in 1957. The federal government takes over $4 billion of this amount while the provincial governments and the municipal governments take just under $1 billion each. Roughly 57 per cent of the five million taxpayers covered by this survey paid 25 per cent of the total taxes collected. They are in the $4,000 and under group. I do not think we should lose sight of this. It is interesting to note that these people contributed about 23 per cent of the federal revenue and 26 per cent of provincial revenue, but that at the municipal level they contributed no less than 34 per cent. This would indicate that the people in the lower income group, the little people, pay more to government at municipal level than they do to either of the other two levels of government. It is also interesting to note on reading this survey that people in the group $7,000 and over pay 40 per cent of the aggregate of all taxes. But this time the pattern is reversed. They pay almost 43 per cent to the federal government, 40 per cent to the provincial government and 30 per cent to the municipalities.
Let us put it in another way. Seventy per cent of all municipal taxes in Canada are collected from those with incomes of $4,000 or less, so any relief in respect of municipal taxes helps the lower income groups first- the labouring man, the farmer, the low income worker with a small family, people who need more help than any other group. These are the men we must be interested in; we must see that their families, their children, are looked after.
It seems to me somewhat archaic that we should not allow any exemptions in income tax in respect of municipal taxation. I think a change in this respect is long overdue.

Similarly, we do not allow income tax deductions in respect of interest paid by a home owner on a mortgage, this is a situation which I believe needs attention right away. In the United States, both municipal taxes and mortgage interest are allowable deductions. Action on these lines would do a good deal to help the small fellow to own his own home and to have a stake in his country.
To follow this theme further, it would seem to me that even without the aid of a municipal bank the chartered banks should, on a well secured loan-the security being, for instance, taxes which are to be paid or government grants due to be received-be able to lend money at a preferred rate of interest. I say this because such loans are virtually guaranteed.
I should like to touch on two other matters briefly. The first is the cancellation of the free testing for brucellosis by the federal authorities. Surely, this is a federal health campaign and in any public health venture the federal government as well as provincial governments should carry a share of the responsibility. Work of this nature for the health of animals has always been under the jurisdiction of the federal government. I need hardly point out that we export cattle to almost every country in the world and that our cattle are considered to be of the highest quality wherever they are sold. I hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) will be able to give this matter his attention very shortly so that farmers can have their cattle tested free of charge.
May I call it six o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, to recapitulate on brucellosis testing, about which I was speaking at the supper recess, this is in my opinion a public health measure designed originally to protect the people from developing the disease, and second, to keep cattle from developing it. Once they developed it breeding programs became severely hampered, and human beings who contracted the disease underwent a long period of illness and convalescence. The loss of young cattle was crippling financially to many farmers. The federal government carried on this testing successfully over the years. Now, at the fruition of this long campaign, it appears that they want to give it up; they want to drop it. I feel that as a health measure this is completely wrong, that the public health
The Address-Mr. Rynard should be protected, and the health of animals branch should continue testing cattle, where possible employing local veterinarians which would cut down the cost of travel and expense. Canada has made great strides over the years in listed and certified cattle. Our cattle have been sold in many parts of the world and have always given a good account of themselves. As a matter of fact, Canada holds an enviable position in this particular field, a fact to which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) will testify. I would hope that he will give this matter his very earliest reconsideration.
I should now like to turn to another matter and to mention briefly the link between cigarette smoking and cancer of the lung. I mentioned this matter some years ago in the house, and since that time mounting evidence has come to light to prove the existence of this link between cigarette smoking and cancer of the lung. The British College of Physicians and Surgeons came out flatfooted last year and stated that cigarette smoking and lung cancer are definitely linked. This year the Canadian Medical Association and the cancer committee of that association have started war on smoking and lung cancer. Surely our federal health department will wait no longer to inform our school children and adults of the dangers of smoking. It has already been stated in an excellent article, I believe by Mr. Burton of the Toronto Star Weekly, that cancer of the lung kills more people than any other single disease. It kills more people than all the traffic accidents and drownings occurring across Canada each year. And once you have contracted this disease your chances of cure are pretty slim indeed. The president of the Canadian Medical Association has stated that this disease has reached epidemic proportions. This suffering and wastage of human life must be stopped. Each day 500 of our young boys and girls in our schools across the land, it is said, commence smoking and many will be condemned to premature death and suffering unless something is done to stop this epidemic of lung cancer.
Mr. Speaker, this is one of the diseases to which we have the answer. It is one of the diseases which starts largely in our schools. To recapitulate, I believe the figure quoted in one of our papers was that 500 boys and girls across Canada start smoking each and every day of the school year. About 100,000 of those children will probably be condemned to death by this disease. Many authors are writing good articles about this disease. There was an excellent article in the Star Weekly and another in the Consumers Digest pointing out the risks and dangers entailed

The Address-Mr. Laniel when one commences to smoke. It is high time that the federal Department of National Health and Welfare joined hands with associations and groups to help bring to the people of Canada not only what is their right to know, but something that may save them from sickness, suffering and probable death.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that it is my sincere hope, and 1 know it is the hope of all Canadians, that the Prime Minister, at the end of his tenure of office, will be able to hand over the affairs of this country in as buoyant a condition as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) handed them over to him.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take this opportunity to congratulate you on your appointment and would beg you to convey my heartiest congratulations to the Speaker of the house for the honour bestowed upon him.
All members of the House of Commons are happy with the manner in which you have presided over the debates until now. Your sense of justice and integrity are in keeping with your high function and a credit to the constituency of Stormont.
I pay tribute also to the movers of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Miss Jewett and Mr. Choquette), who discharged their duties with ease and spirit.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to take part in this debate, because I too wished to express in this chamber the feelings of confidence I have had since the change of government. Moreover, those feelings are shared by all the Canadian people, who for many months had wanted to get out of this period of insecurity and indecision brought upon us by the Conservative regime.
There are two ways to examine the present situation and, consequently, the legislative program of the government, as outlined in the speech from the throne. We can enumerate the legislative measures mentioned, comment upon them and show to what extent they measure up to the expectations of the Canadian people, or we can compare the present situation with the one that prevailed at the opening of the twenty fifth parliament. I will adopt the latter procedure and go back to the 1962 election campaign when the party in power then was on the defensive, trying to justify itself and hoping for even half a victory, wishing to keep enough seats to form a government, even a minority government. They had to cling to power at all costs, forgetting that the people had the right to know about our economic situation and our relations with the rest of the world. I will not
[Mr. Rynard.l

go over all the events but the facts prove that our leaders had failed to assume their responsibilities.
A second party which had been selling soap on television for two years, Social Credit, had certainly built up a clientele in part of the province of Quebec. During the election campaign, they kept on being as constructive and they hammered into the people's minds that they had nothing to lose, that they did not have to understand the Social Credit doctrine and, surprisingly enough, some people believed them. However, they forgot one thing. You cannot forever take a negative attitude and the last election proved it.
The "anti" this and "anti" that campaign lost a lot of speed since last April 8.
Mr. Speaker, it is fun to go to the circus but being part of one is another thing.
As for the New Democratic party, the grandson of the C.C.F. and the last offspring of the P.S.D., it remains as always conscious of its role as a watchdog. There are good men in that party but do they really believe that they will one day form the government of Canada?
As for our party, and here I am still referring to the election campaign of 1962, after a keen contest with the Conservatives, showing their mistakes and their irresolution, as compared to the program that we were offering them, the leader of the Liberal party demanded immediate action and requested a quick convening of the chambers.
We were defending parliament's rights to study urgent problems and we questioned some of the things done by government members.
All those people, Mr. Speaker, came to the opening of parliament on September 27, to listen to a speech from the throne that offered nothing new and a Prime Minister who was often arrogant. Before this Conservative intransigence, we, the Liberals, deemed it our duty to defend the people and we came to the conclusion that at that time the only weapon available to us was to overthrow that government which was considering only its own political interests.
The three other parties have accused us of engaging in petty politics, of refusing to give a chance to the Conservatives, who had not been able to accomplish, with more than 200 members-the strongest majority in the house since confederation-what they claimed

they could accomplish successfully with a minority government, but without even wanting to discuss matters with the opposition.
While the N.D.P. members were seeking to have their leader elected in a by-election and in a province that was not even his, the Social Credit members, saviours of the French Canadian race, were discovering that they had a nationalist mission, among all the contradictions and the endless sermons on a mock money system. They always tried to hold up to ridicule our institutions and our qualified authorities. All the speeches delivered by the member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) during the last election campaign had already been given in the house during that short session. In fact, a journalist wrote in La Presse on January 30, 1963 and I quote:
To have the Social Crediters in the house is too high a price to pay for what we are gaining in terms of bilingualism.
We, Liberals, might not have been in the headlines as often as those who were shouting; we have had perhaps a little more than our share of criticisms, but this does not mean that we have been inactive, on the contrary.
We had taken a decision in the face of the inefficiency of the Conservative government, and, during that period we were preparing ourselves to replace them. Our action was much more positive than certain people believed it was, and today the record shows that we have sought long term solutions to our problems. This can be seen from our program during the last election campaign and from the speech from the throne. It is all very well to be shocked by a unilingual menu at the cafeteria; it is still better to ask that Beauchesne be translated, if this is possible; but what can be gained by claiming Donald Gordon's head? Especially if the system is not changed, or if such an individual is replaced by his like.
Can we infer that a joint Liberal action, even if it is unnoticed, is worthless?
Some people have claimed that Social Credit is positive nationalism; it might seem that way to the Quebec voters, who elected 26 Crediters out of a total of 30. Yet is the speech delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on biculturalism on December 17 not really positive action? And who could have brought about such a broad outlook among the leaders of the Liberal party but the team of our members, people who know how to dialogue, who are trying to understand each other and to act accordingly?
The Address-Mr. Laniel
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to serve my country on such a team under the leadership of such a competent and understanding leader as the present Prime Minister. Besides, several Conservatives are envious of us or have been in the past.
We have all examined the speech from the throne in which we find promising legislation for the future. Let the Conservatives make fun of the 60 days of decision promised by our party. They cannot understand such a thing, it is new to them. They are amazed to realize that the best way to solve a problem is to face it without delay. This is what the Liberal party intends to do within the next four years. Moreover, the Prime Minister clearly stated on many occasions that those 60 days are the first 60 days of decision suggesting thereby that this is only the beginning. We can feel already an atmosphere of confidence, we treat our friends as such, we call things by their names, the word "unemployment" is spoken once again and we are not afraid to use it while seeking the means to check it, especially if we consider that the Leader of the Opposition has finally managed to take a definite stand on the matter of nuclear weapons.
We repeat in this house what we have preached during the election campaign and a part of it has even been mentioned in the speech from the throne. We are ready to assume our responsibilities although it is obvious that we have many problems to solve and that many questions will require much tact.
Mr. Speaker, I admit frankly that there is no magic way of solving the problem of biculturalism but this government has resolved to create an equal partnership between the English speaking and the French speaking people. In the speech he delivered on May 20 in this house, the Prime Minister has shown his firm intention regarding this question and has said that the Canadian entity would progress only through the co-ordinated efforts of each and every one of us.
But you cannot have a bicultural country without having a country. So Quebec, to be Quebec, must be Quebec in Canada.
Such are the words spoken by the present Prime Minister.
As far as I am concerned, I am ready to negotiate and most Canadians feel the same. I am confident in Canada's future, I believe in the possibility of a truly bilingual country where citizens of both major racial groups would have equal opportunities without infringing upon the rights of other minorities.

The Address-Mr. Irvine order labour to accept specific jobs in specific communities and at specific rates of pay.
That is what a planned economy means in its extreme form and this is what the Liberal economic council may mean. No government can plan for full employment with any real hope of implementing that plan unless it has some power to order and direct. It might further be contended that even this ultimate form of state planning and state control cannot be wholly effective, for the simple reason that Canada cannot live in isolation; for the simple reason that this country, however the government might seek to direct its economy, will remain vulnerable to economic influences from beyond her own borders.
I am not alone in this thought. The financial community is disturbed by the vague generality of the information contained in the throne speech. Labour too is showing signs of concern. Just as no businessman is willing to abdicate in favour of management by bureaucracy, so it is that no worker in Canada with an investment in home and family life in any community is prepared to sell, to move and to start anew in another part of the country at the dictates of this or any other government.
The throne speech indicates that the government proposes to establish a national development fund. Here again the vague general statement of intention has caused concern in the business community and among financial institutions. For a government that made a campaign boast of restoring national stability, the administration appears to be doing its utmost to accomplish just exactly the reverse.
What is this development fund to be? Is it to be a gigantic government mutual fund, with its resources drawn from the major financial institutions and the small investor? Will this government sponsored agency divert investment funds, again by some form of compulsion? Or, if it offers inducements to big and small investors, then will it in fact compete with its own bond issues? Will it compete with provincial and municipal governments for investment capital? These are questions we would be well advised to ask ourselves and dwell on before we make a fatal step.
The third element in the government's economic program is that of calling for the establishment of a municipal loan fund. Municipalities naturally would welcome an ever ready, ever available source of low cost financing for local projects, and I would like to add here that I am sure the London council would be very pleased with something like that. I have had some experience with them on this subject.

I gather that the government has in mind a revolving fund of perhaps some $400 million, with a forgiveness clause applicable to municipalities that complete works within specific time limits. This at first glance might appear attractive. Indeed municipal governments have long advocated such a federal program. However it should be noticed that the proposed plan appears to be merely an extension of the present government's system of loans, but with the added feature of making a new board the central clearing house for all applications.
It will be interesting to see if the legislation confers any greater benefit upon the municipalities than does the winter works program of the previous government. This was a virtually all embracing program, and it should be remembered that under it municipalities derived a substantial benefit in the federal government's share of the labour costs involved. It remains to be seen if the municipalities will be happier with interest bearing loans than with the shared cost arrangement of the previous government.
Mr. Speaker, the government party's stolen slogan of "60 days of decision" has in fact provided a 60 day honeymoon for the new administration, but the honeymoon is just about over. The government must soon face the harsh realities of living with the inflated promises to which it was wedded in the zeal of an extravagant election campaign. How extravagant it was we already have had some intimation in the throne speech, with its forecast of a multiplicity of boards, funds and bureaucrats. Just how costly all this may be we will, I presume, learn in the budget next month.
The government is committed to effecting a closer balance between revenues and expenditures, and to moving towards a balanced budget.
The Prime Minister in his 1962 campaign promised a balanced budget within two years of assuming office. Presumably this means that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will go half way in his 1963-64 budget toward striking the promised balance. With the current tempo of the economy he has a favourable tide flowing his way. The house will await the budget as a measure of not only government responsibility in office, but of Liberal responsibility when out of office.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that with the present composition of the House of Commons we are in a position where, if we get down to the task at hand, we should and could have good, sound administration. The members on the opposition side of the house will see to it that this happens. Over the period of the last six years we have enjoyed an economic growth

never before experienced in Canada in peacetime. We are turning the country over to the new government in an extremely sound condition, and I would say that now is the time for us, whether we sit on the east or the west side of the chamber, to put nation first and party second. Let us get together in a spirit of progress and co-operation and get on with the business of running the country. (Translation):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with custom and tradition, 1 must first offer my congratulations to the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker and also to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Miss Jewett and Mr. Choquette), who have performed their duties so well.
We are undertaking here a task which is most serious. From the start this first session of the twenty sixth parliament has new horizons to contemplate concerning our country's economy.
During the last election campaign, a great many projects were brought up for the benefit of Canadians from coast to coast.
The fact that the responsibility for administering the affairs of the state has been handed over to those who were so pessimistic, as we found out during the previous session, which lasted but 71 days and ended last February, seems to have stimulated them so much that they have become as optimistic as it is possible to be.
Canada's future and the future of Canadians must be considered from an angle which is sufficiently idealistic, even if the speech from the throne is rather vague with regard to the announcements and matters we will have to discuss during this brief session, to give us great hopes for Canada and all our fellow citizens from sea to sea.
Evidently, some things may be more pressing than others. I realize that, following an election, which, like the last one we had, consisted in a rapid attack, where all sorts of arrows were aimed against us in Quebec, who had to take more than we could absorb, we might tend to retaliate. I shall not waste my time pointing out all those barbed and pointed attacks against us. However, let me mention a few allusions made by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel), who, a few moments ago, mentioned the "funny free money" of the Social Crediters.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that it has been more or less seriously tried to cast discredit upon what the Social Credit party has been advocating throughout the country for many years, i.e. the essential need to revise this country's
The Address-Mr. Perron Bank Act so that money might become an instrument of service in the hands of the shareholders, that is our society as a whole. I submit that nobody in this house has the right to try casting a slight upon us by speaking of "free money", when it is known that, among the many economists who, today, are sitting on the government benches nobody has yet been able to find a formula for reviving our economy. I hope we will be submitted other things than magic formulas, to amuse Canadians in general, and the whole country from coast to coast-formulas which are nothing but a waste of time-to solve this country's problems, which are great and many.
As the member for Beauce, which I have again the privilege of representing in this house, I can speak on behalf of French Canadians, and more particularly those of my own province. I also speak on my own behalf. I do not want to commit the group to which I belong, but I believe that, after the unfortunate events which recently took place in my province, it is high time that we consider, from all possible angles, the various problems which our Canadian society will have to face.
Speaking as a patriotic Canadian, I wish to be well understood by all, tonight.
It is all very well during an election campaign, to try to discredit an opponent, but the day has come now, I feel, to assume our responsibilities as right-minded Canadians and look seriously to the future of our country.
Much has been said about the state of Quebec. There has been much talk about it. In some Quebec circles, people have talked about the magic formula of Social Credit.
But will economists, at least those who are now among the fighting wing of the government party, be able to find something besides the formulas of indebtedness which we have known.
The speech from the throne mentions the setting up of a municipal development board. Will this be done according to the concept of conventional economists, that is by borrowing at 5 per cent to lend to municipalities at 1 per cent? That would only displace the uneasiness, since they should tax indirectly to pay the heavy burden of interest that we already have to repay on the huge amount of indebtedness we have all over Canada: federal, provincial, municipal and school debts.
As a Quebecer, I know something of the problems of our beautiful province. The indebtedness has no end. The critical economic

The Address-Mr. Perron situation in which they struggle at all levels of administration of public affairs is unimaginable.
As far as our school boards are concerned, the parent commission in the province of Quebec claims that an amount between $4 and $5 million should be used in the next few years to prepare plans enabling us to develop the talents of our people in the intellectual field as well as in the technical and scientific fields.
We have also been talking of steel mills for over ten or 15 years in the province of Quebec. What is preventing the establishment of those secondary industries which would convert our own raw material on our own soil and put to work a great part of our manpower and, consequently, would help to curb the unemployment evil which exists at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, this beautiful province of Quebec, for the past three or four years, had held the unemployment record. In January only, there were 200,000 unemployed in the beautiful province of Quebec, while at the same time many hundreds of persons could not keep their arms busy throughout the country. It was impossible to build factories on our own soil in order to bring wealth to the whole Canadian community, yet, during that time, under the cover of social security, what was happening? One hundred and thirty two million dollars were being spent on social welfare, while numerous inquiries were being made to try, not to find means to end dire poverty, but rather to deprive thousands of people from the benefits of legislation which could have afforded them the opportunity of providing their families with the bread and butter they lacked.
What is offered to us? A municipal development and loan board, and an area development agency. All these boards exist already at the provincial level and we have many of them. A corporation to finance the tremendous works which must be undertaken in the province of Quebec has also been established as we did here last year when we considered the Atlantic development board, discussing the matter for days.
What prevents the carrying out of all these things, even if it has been said that it will require lots of imagination to get the economy moving again?
I believe that we have in our province as well as in the other provinces, businessmen who think big and who have enough im-

agination to assess the needs of the people and our own processing and manufacturing capabilities according to our people's wishes and needs.
Is there today in the country a shortage of the basic things needed by the consumer?
I am not talking about food and clothing. Of course I do not mention housing because I feel that it is time to find solutions to take out of the slums of Montreal, Quebec city and other cities in Canada, large families who must live there.
How many families worry about tomorrow, not because there is a shortage of goods but rather because the consumer does not have the means to buy what we could produce.
How many things could we produce ourselves to meet the demand if the consumers could pay for what they need?
Chambers of commerce, study groups and all kinds of commissions try to find solutions to those economic problems and a policy that would create new jobs. But, in the meantime, while talking about industrialization, we do nothing for some people who are underfed because they are unable to find work in their own country.
This state of affairs exists in my own constituency because we do not have the possibility of establishing secondary plants that could employ most of the manpower in Beauce. In that riding which has been in existence for 250 years, these North American pioneers even had to go into exile in other provinces and even out of Canada to find work.
Last fall some people talked here-and we will hear it again-of the protection we must give our workers who must go and earn their living in the state of Maine, south of the border. Why is it not possible to use some imagination and get the economy moving again inasmuch as money will not interfere with the plans of our administrators, at the municipal or school board level as well as at the provincial level?
It is all very well to laugh at the Social Crediters' "free money", but I think that the people are rather entitled to laugh at the lack of serious solutions by our economists to the many problems which at present face our society. It is not easy to find formulas to solve these problems. It is not by blaming formulas that problems can be solved.

The state of Quebec is on the march. We do not ask for more than our fair share but we want French Canadians to feel at home within the Canadian confederation so that they may march forward as equal partners in this twentieth century.
As a great leader of the Liberal party once said, the twentieth century belongs to Canada. If we want that to become a reality, Mr. Speaker, our own financial institutions will have to start working in the interest of the Canadian people instead of against them as they always did in the past.
At present, the processing of our raw materials is done outside of Canada, thus giving work to foreigners, after which the finished product is sold back to us at a profit. During the election campaign, the Liberal candidates often quoted from page 11 of their official propaganda booklet which reads as follows:
A new Liberal government will fully ensure that the money supply is adequate and that business is not crippled through a lack of credit.
What then is preventing our province from undertaking without delay, like the other nine Canadian provinces, a great number of projects, since plans have already been made at the provincial or municipal level to develop our economy?
What is preventing the carrying out of these many projects, if not the lack of funds or credit facilities available to those organizations willing to undertake those projects in order to give a new start to the Canadian economy?
The speech from the throne also mentions the matter of biculturalism and great emphasis was placed on the subject during the election campaign. The matter has been entrusted to the worthy representative for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Lamontagne) who will set up the commission appointed to look fully into the matter.
I wonder if the people of Quebec will have confidence in that commission when they realize who is responsible for it? After reading his works, one finds that provincial governments become branches of the central power, and such a stand is taken on the authority of the Rowell-Sirois report, which is perhaps the most centralizing of all royal inquiries.
Following that commission's report, centralization was put into effect by the Liberals
The Address-Mr. Perron who held office at the time and who, between 1940 and 1945, took away bit by bit, piece by piece, from the province of Quebec, the resources which would have enabled her to assume her responsibilities in the field of social security.
Unfortunately, we still meet Canadians who claim that it is the French Canadians' fault if they do not hold in confederation the place they should but that they had to relinquish in certain fields. Why? What prevented the provinces from availing themselves of the advantages offered in the field of social security, if not the financial impossibility of meeting objectives which the twentieth century has set throughout the world?
So, as a French Canadian from Quebec, I sincerely hope that the commission on biculturalism will be something more than a toy good for a couple of years, that is until we celebrate the confederation centennial in 1967, at the time the world fair is to be held in the province of Quebec.
As the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Pepin) was saying, I do hope that this will not be another opportunity to have us miss the boat. We would not want to miss the boat once again. We are now in full "evolution" and, please note, I do not say "revolution". We want Quebec to have its share in confederation. We wish to have our say, economically and politically, on a national basis and even on a world wide basis. We want a Canada where we shall be able to live in accordance with the legitimate aspirations of human beings who lack security but still hold the greatest respect for freedom.
Security and freedom are exemplary things to be carried very high today, because, under the cover of freedom and security, whole nations have been crushed under the boots of dictators. The economic dictatorship to which we are subjected at the present time may not be for our fellow Canadians as crushing as the political dictatorship some peoples have had to live under. While, in the name of authority, dictators have reduced peoples to slavery, I do not believe that we have the right, in the name of freedom, to allow democracy to take advantage of the masses, as it happens in this Canada of ours.
Many family heads, farmers and factory workers, citizens from large cities and small towns, had put their confidence in the future of our country. How many businessmen now

The Address-Mr. Perron realize that everything is not running smoothly in their country?
Let us talk now about contradictions. The speech from the throne mentions the appointment of a second minister of agriculture, a French Canadian representing the Atlantic provinces and better acquainted with the problems of the eastern farmers, and at the same time the present Minister of Agriculture announces the abolition of the milk subsidy. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if this is a policy likely to give new confidence to the French Canadian people of Quebec and I wonder if our Canadian confederation does not still operate to our disadvantage because I represent a group of people composed of large French Canadian families who had to leave home and go here and there, due to the lack of job opportunities in their native place, in their own county.
We have had imaginative people who succeeded in building firms with a national and international reputation. I could give as an example the "Vachon" cakes from Ste. Marie de Beauce. There are still in Canada businessmen with imagination in our twentieth century. If only loans were made available to them through an industrial financing bank. At the present time we have an industrial development bank which refuses to grant 75 per cent of the loans requested. If money were more readily available, if it were within the reach of these businessmen, we would see the industrial situation change in our country and there would be created additional jobs. I wish the province of Quebec would nc longer hold this notorious unemployment record in Canada.
During the last election campaign, and generally, much has been said about the fact that the province of Quebec has delivered an ultimatum. And it is still being repeated. According to that ultimatum, there are only ten months left to give back to the province of Quebec part of its tax rights, that is 25 per cent of individual income tax, 25 per cent of corporate income tax and 100 per cent of the estate tax. How many of us have realized that two months have already gone by since that 12-month ultimatum was given? It seems that some would like to forget it.
It was said during the last election campaign that our magic formulas had no value at all. Maybe they prefer to keep bowing tc the financiers in this country, those who control money and finance everywhere, under the banking system we have in Canada. Canadians are being paralysed and prevented from making this country a place where people

would smile more often instead of being concerned about the future.
We have witnessed a radical change in the speeches made in the house. Last year, the Liberal party took pleasure in blaming the Conservative party in a most pessimistic way, sometimes to the point of preventing businessmen from being confident about our industries, because they feared the financial future of the country. This same party is now most optimistic. Is this the justification of what we had been advocating for several years already? Are the good parties good only when they sit on the opposition benches?
Mr. Speaker, I hope we will find out the worth of some who, today, assume administrative responsibilities in the affairs of Canada. The party in power must stop acting like the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) who tried to hold us up to ridicule. He should not forget that as the representative of a riding in a minority government, he must also, like myself, represent the interests of all Canadians, and it is with the sincerity of a politician that we must strive toward that objective, and not by running down the splinter parties or by predicting that there is no future for them.
Social Credit has contributed its own pinpricks. Today, in Quebec, things are moving since June 18, even though nobody will give us the credit of having awakened the nationalist feelings of French Canada.
I do not feel obliged to say that it is not only by insisting on a bilingual menu in the cafeteria that we will reach our objective, because we have seen behind that something besides bilingualism. We have seen something else there and, moreover, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) said himself, a few months before the election campaign, that the French Canadians in Quebec will no longer be satisfied with bilingual cheques. We have also seen something besides bilingualism. We have seen two great nations, the very foundation of that confederation, which want to go forward together. It has been repeated that the best thing was to make Canada from coast to coast a country where it is good to live, a country able to give security and freedom to each and every one of its citizens.
We do not call for magic formulas which would free us from economic servitude but we ask that a sound monetary system based on mathematical data be set up to bring about a constant balance between production and

consumption, under which money would not stand in the way of those who can make our country richer and more productive and who want to show the whole world that people of various nationalities can live together in a country where bilingualism is recognized by the constitution itself.
Mr. Speaker, my opinion concerning the French fact may be different from that of your predecessor who feels that French Canadians should be on the same footing as newly arrived Canadians in this country. In my opinion, there is quite a difference between one's right to be educated in one's mother tongue and to speak it and the right of equal partnership in this fine and great country of America which is recognized by the constitution.
That is why, on behalf of all Canadians, I would ask those who are entrusted with the government of our country to provide, not the magic formulas they claimed to have, but at least down to earth solutions. The numerous economists who are members of the government should find means to restore the confidence of the people in a political climate where we could rightly expect the fulfilment of the predictions that the twentieth century would belong to Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I in this my maiden speech in this house join with other hon. members in congratulating you on your election to your very high office, a position which I know you are very worthy of holding. I should also like to congratulate the Deputy Speaker, who is also chairman of committees, and to join with other hon. members who spoke earlier in complimenting the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. These speeches were two of the finest I have heard this session.
My riding of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare is one of the finest in Canada and is in the finest province, Nova Scotia. This riding consists of three provincial ridings: Shelburne, being a single riding; Yarmouth, a dual riding; and Clare, a single riding. Shelburne county is nearly 100 per cent English speaking. Yarmouth is about 50 per cent French speaking and 50 per cent English speaking and Clare is about 100 per cent French speaking. Most of the people of Shelburne
The Address-Mr. Armstrong county are fishermen, depending for their livelihood mainly on the sea. The town of Lockeport, which is part of Shelburne county, has three fishing plants employing approximately 350 people, both men and women, as fish cutters, packers, and so forth. The fish are brought in by draggers and long-liners, and people from the surrounding area are employed there. In the town of Shelburne the same thing applies as in Lockeport, but the fishing plants are not as large. Another industry in Shelburne is the manufacture of office and school furniture from moulded plywood by Ven-Rez Products Company. Shelburne is also noted for its fine granite stone from which is manufactured in the town tombstones and granite stone sidings for buildings.
The people in the remaining area of Shelburne county are engaged in fishing or in fish plants, with the exception of the areas of Clyde river, Upper Clyde and Ohio, where they are engaged for the most part in lumbering. There are also boat shops in the Shelburne, Shag Harbour and Woods Harbour areas, where they build Cape island lobster boats, which are sold both locally and in the United States.
(Translation):
The people of Clare county depend a great deal on fishing, some on farming, lumbering and boat construction for their livelihood, but families in that part of my riding derive most of their income from fishing. There are several small businesses that build boats from 35 to 50 feet long, many of which are exported to the United States. There are also two large shipyards, each employing about a hundred workers. Those shipyards build boats up to 125 feet long, which are mostly used for scallop fishing and other types of deep sea fishing. Those businesses were set up during the war by the numerous French speaking Acadians who live in that part of my county.
Allow me to say, Mr. Speaker, that the French speaking people of Yarmouth and Clare counties expect to enjoy one day television programs on the French network of the C.B.C. Since you all know the story of the Acadian people, I need not repeat it tonight. You can appreciate as well as I do the importance of French culture and French language media to my Acadian constituents. I read in the papers recently that the C.B.C. was planning to build shortly a satellite station at Cheticamp, in Cape Breton, and in

The Address-Mr. Armstrong the Magdalen islands. I am not familiar with technical problems, but I expect that it would probably be just as easy to build a rebroadcasting station at Digby Neck in order to comply with the rightful demands of our French speaking population.
I trust that my colleagues from the province of Quebec will use their influence with the departmental authorities to help me obtain this satellite station.
There is also in my county the St. Anne college at Pointe de l'Eglise. This college is well known to all Acadians and it has surely helped them to preserve and develop their French culture. The Reverend Eudist Fathers direct the college which is attended by over 300 students. Two months ago, works at a cost of $300,000 were undertaken to receive an additional 150 students. As you see, my French Canadian constituents are active and the French people of my riding are trying to develop with all modern means available.
(Text):
The people of Yarmouth county also depend a lot on fishing, some lumbering and farming. The chief industry we have in the town of Yarmouth is the manufacturing of cotton duck by Cosmos Imperial Mills Limited, who employ approximately 400 people. The other industry is the manufacturing of sweaters and tartan plaids by Thistle Knitwear Company Limited. Then there is in the town of Yarmouth the Yarmouth Ice Cream and Dairy Company Limited, large milk suppliers and manufacturers of butter, cheese, ice cream and various frozen foods.
The communities of Wedgeport and West Pubnico are large fishing areas with their own fish plants. Boats 35 to 50 feet long for lobster fishing and pleasure are also built there and sold in the United States. We also have in West Pubnico a firm engaged in the manufacturing of school buses. In these two areas almost all the people are French speaking.
We also have our problems in Yarmouth. One is the television supplied by the satellite station bringing in a channel from Halifax. Our people are pleased to have this service but are dissatisfied with its extent and have asked me to try to obtain another channel.
Another problem is our local airport which Is becoming outdated and not large enough for the planes that are now being used. We were told before the election of 1962 that $1,600,000 was set aside for an extension to the airport, but since that time nothing has been said or done about it. This apparently is another project affected by the austerity program. If the existing airport in Yarmouth is not enlarged and improved it will mean we will have a feeder service from Halifax or Saint
[Mr. Armstrong.!
John, New Brunswick, possibly two or three times a week, resulting in the worst setback western Nova Scotia has ever had.
For instance, the lobster buyers are working up trade with other countries to ship live lobsters or fresh lobster meat to other parts of Canada and to all parts of the United States. Our tourist trade will also be greatly affected if the project is not carried out. I believe that after this government has looked into the matter something will be done to improve the situation.
We also have the motor vessel Bluenose plying from Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, to Bar Harbor, Maine, making a round trip daily during the summer months and the tourist season. This service began in 1956. We are all delighted to have the Bluenose plying between these two ports, but hotel and motel operators as well as the merchants in Yarmouth believe that the vessel, being Canadian owned and operated by Canadian National Railways with a Canadian crew, should lay over at night at Yarmouth and not at Bar Harbor, Maine. If she did this, tourists would then be in our town during the late afternoon for shopping and would patronize our hotels and motels in Yarmouth overnight. I also intend to bring this matter to the attention of the government.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, my riding is essentially a district of primary industries. With regard to the primary industries of fishing and the gathering of Irish moss, in going around the area I find that the requirements for these have been neglected in the past three years. More and improved facilities are needed because each year more boats are being built and more people are entering the fishing. In most cases throughout the area the wharves and breakwaters, which were barely adequate 10 years ago, have not been improved or enlarged, making the facilities completely inadequate for the increased number of boats being used each year. Our fishermen do not want handouts but are seeking decent facilities to protect their boats and equipment.
It is gratifying to know, Mr. Speaker, that our Prime Minister, who has been in office such a short time, has already visited the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the President of the United States of America, and has had friendly and constructive discussions with them. In my opinion there is no better way to live and prosper than to be friendly with one's neighbours.
I am pleased to see included in the throne speech the item to reduce barriers limiting trade. This is a step in the right direction, especially with regard to trade with the

United States, as our people in Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare are almost totally dependant on the United States for markets for their fish, Irish moss and other products.
The establishment of a 12-mile limit is something that has been talked about for years but nothing has ever been done. I am pleased to see that the present government is endeavouring to implement this undertaking which, if brought into being, will be so beneficial to our Canadian fishermen.
The people of Canada, I am sure, will be pleased with the establishment of a comprehensive contributory pension plan, and I do expect the government to increase as soon as possible existing old age pensions and old age assistance payments as well as pensions for the blind and disabled to $75 a month, and also to extend the provisions to single women and widows at the age of 60.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I am proud to be a member of this house and to be associated with such a fine group of people from all parties. I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister upon having selected a very capable group of cabinet ministers. My aim now is to endeavour to do the job the voters of Shelburne-Yarmouth -Clare expect me to do.
