speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to add my congratulations to the many you have already received upon your election to the high position of presiding over the debates of this house. I am sure that you will continue to enjoy the confidence of the members on all sides of the house for many years to come. I should like also to extend my congratulations to the mover (Miss Jewett) and the seconder (Mr. Choquette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I should like to extend my congratulations to all those members who have been returned to this parliament. It is said that the battle of opinions is the true dialogue of democracy. We are all believers in democracy in this house. I think all of us form friendships with members of all parties. It is one of the great pleasures of being re-elected to renew those friendships.
For a moment, I should like to make some observations about the composition of this house. I have been very amused during the last few days to watch the Liberal backbenchers and see member after member in the back row get up and make his maiden speech. I think this is a very fine thing. Indeed, this privilege is not easily won, because in the last parliament one of the members sitting in the back benches complained very bitterly over the fact that a small group of frontbenchers prevented him from speaking, asked that speeches be
The Address-Mr. Slogan censored, and so forth. I sometimes wonder how altruistic this freedom of the backbenchers in the Liberal party is. I have waited to hear some of the members on the front benches speak. I thought that after all of this talk about action and decision, one by one the ministers would get up and say: This is the policy of action for Canada. They have been very mute indeed. It seems to me that they are merely using the backbenchers to hide their own lack of policy. In fact, their policy seems ephemeral indeed, because it seems to dissolve day by day as the 60-day period dissolves.
I should like to make a brief comment on the composition of the cabinet. A few days ago I was in Toronto attending the Canadian Dental Association convention. During that time I took the opportunity of visiting some of my friends who belong to different ethnic groups. I must say that these days they all seem to be Liberals. They expressed very keen disappointment in this government because the very able member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) who, on the basis of seniority should have been appointed to the cabinet, had been overlooked. I believe the Prime Minister was asked to put him in the cabinet. He would have made a very wonderful minister of health, but instead of that the Prime Minister relegated him to the position of caddy to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh). There are other fine members on the other side of the house. There is the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) and the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso). These are members who represent that third force in Canadian life about which the other side of the house has been so mute. I refer to the one quarter of the Canadian people who are not of Anglo-Saxon or French descent. For 22 years, the Liberals ignored them. The very able member for Vegreville sat here for eight years but received no recognition at all.
How different it was when the Conservative party came to power. The former minister of labour was appointed immediately, and he was one of the finest ministers of labour this country has ever had. We now have an Indian senator and there are two Ukrainian senators, one representing each faith. We are all waiting to see what this government is going to do about this third force to which they pay such great lip service. The present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) were so loudly indignant. They said the Conservatives always talked about this third force in Canadian life. They said they were the ones who really represented these people. Well, these people are waiting. I am sorry that I have to be the one to speak for those who are

The Address-Mr. Slogan in Toronto, but obviously the present members from Toronto are not looking after them.
In any'event, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the Liberal frontbenchers will pay a great deal of attention to the backbenchers and also the opposition, because they ought to do so. You know, the backbenchers are an indis-pensible lot these days and their price comes rather high as the Liberals have found out. They are not easily bought. It is a fact that the opposition represents the opinions of 57 per cent of the people of Canada. The government, therefore, should pay more attention to the opposition than to their own policies, policies that were rejected by the majority of the Canadian people, as were the majority of the Liberal candidates.
I do not want to be so negative all the time. I want to tell you a little bit about that great Conservative party and the policies that party has followed. These policies have, all too often, been misunderstood by our friends and misrepresented by those who are opposed to us. The Conservative party was born long before Canada. In 1854 a young lawyer by the name of John A. Macdonald united a group of progressive young men behind his dynamic leadership. This was a group of men with differing views but a common purpose. That purpose was to unite the existing colonies which were disorganized and were being threatened externally. He set about bringing confederation into effect and creating the nation of Canada. Thirteen years later that nation was created, largely on the initiative of the Conservative party. Sir John A. Macdonald, the first prime minister of Canada, did not rest then. He had another vision, a vision of extending and uniting this Canada from sea to sea. In order to accomplish this, the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway was undertaken.
This was the greatest single feat in Canadian history. It dwarfs the St. Lawrence seaway. Almost 100 years later we are just opening the trans-Canada highway. The defeatist Grit opposition of the day said we were building railways from tepee to tepee. I have just introduced this little bit of history in order to show that the policy of the Conservative party has always been a Canada first policy, a policy of national purpose and national unity.
I am not going to give you a history lesson tonight, but I should like to refer to 1957. After 22 years of Liberal government, confederation was beginning to split at the seams. The leader of the Conservative party said to the people of Canada: This party wants to provide equality of opportunity for all parts of the country, to all segments of the people and to all segments of the economy. He said


that there were certain parts of the country which had fallen behind and he named those parts. He referred to the maritimes, the west and the north. He said that there were certain segments of the people who had fallen behind, and he named them. These were the people on fixed income. They were falling behind because the cost of living index was going up at a rate of 3.7 per cent per year over the last 10 years of the Liberal regime, and their meagre pensions were being eaten up. These were the old age pensioners, the blind, the disabled, the veterans, the Indian population and so forth. He said there were certain segments of the economy falling behind, and he mentioned small business and agriculture.
Then we said what we would do about it, and when we were elected in 1957 we started to do something about it. We immediately raised old age pensions by a further $9 a month. Mr. Speaker, you have heard about the six buck boys. It might be interesting for hon. members on the other side of the house to realize that the Liberal government was defeated on June 10 of that year, and the increase of $6 did not come into effect until July 1, so that we paid for that six bucks, and immediately afterwards increased old age pensions by a further $9 a month, and later still by a further $10 a month. This has meant well over $1 million in the pockets of old age pensioners in my riding alone annually.
Old age assistance, together with the blind, disabled and veterans pensions were also raised, and we did something for the Indian people. We appointed an Indian senator and we gave the Indians the vote. They had the vote in eastern Canada at one time, but in 1898 the Liberal government took it away from them.
We improved their housing, and if one doubts what I am saying all he has to do is go through any Indian reserve in my riding where there are 3,500 Indians, to see the improvements in education, in new schools, new houses, new roads being built, and in the new self-help projects such as pulp wood cooperatives. We adopted a progressive attitude towards these people who had fallen behind. We have heard a lot about the Glassco report and integration of Indian schools and hospitals. This is already taking place in my riding. These are some of the things I just want to mention in passing.
Then we dealt with the segments of the economy which had fallen behind. This included small business, and for the first time the government introduced small business loans, to help small businessmen get loans of up to $25,000 to improve their premises and assist them compete in modern society.
With regard to agriculture we displayed the same basic approach to it as we brought

to bear on all the problems of Canada. What are the problems in agriculture? Mr. Speaker, you know what they are. The unpredictability of the weather is one of them, and so we broadened the eligibility for P.F.A.A. and increased the payments. We brought in crop insurance. To cope with the problem of surpluses we introduced the accelerated sales program. There was a shortage of credit, and so we scrapped the old farm loan board and set up the Farm Credit Corporation. Under the old board an average of $4 million a year was lent to farmers during the Liberal regime, but under the Farm Credit Corporation loans to farmers last year alone amounted to $90 million more. These are the kind of things we did to extend credit to farmers; yet the Liberal party says it is going to extend credit to farmers.
There was instability of prices and to deal with that we brought in the Prices Stabilization Act. We also introduced ARDA. I could tell you the story of wheat-the greatest story ever told. When we signed the Chinese wheat agreement the then hon. member for Assini-boia said "This is not a deal because there is no fixed price." Do hon. members not remember the British wheat deal signed by the Liberal government, which robbed western farmers of $600 million? Well, we were not going to make that mistake; we did not want a fixed price.
The price of wheat was $1.67 a bushel when the Chinese agreement was signed. Afterwards it went up to over $2 a bushel, and that meant millions of dollars more in the pockets of the western farmers without costing the taxpayers a cent. When the farmers marched on Ottawa they asked for a subsidy of 30 cents a bushel. In the end result they got more and it did not cost the taxpayers a cent.
Liberal spokesmen have talked about a minimum price of $2 a bushel. Mr. Argue, when he came into Springfield, went one better. He said $3 a bushel for wheat under the two price system for the first 300 bushels, and a guaranteed minimum of $2 a bushel for the rest. Mr. Speaker, I am all for that, and I am just waiting for it to be implemented.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister promised free milk for school children. We have a big milk surplus and so he said they would give free milk to all the children in schools. We are still waiting for that. All sorts of promises were made to agriculture. One of the promises was a higher initial payment on oats and barley to be announced before seeding time. Well, seeding time is here but the announcement is not. It just goes to show this government is not
The Address-Mr. Slogan a government of decision or action. It is a government of inaction and a government that is trying to forget its promises.
I am not going to talk much about agriculture because many able agricultural spokesmen have spoken before me, but it is a sad story indeed that we have to have two ministers of agriculture. In fact the one minister we have has nothing to do now because he is going to auction sales. The government has not enough activity to keep one minister occupied. The farmers of western and eastern Canada are not looking forward to the fragmentation of the national policies for agriculture brought in by the previous government.
We said that certain parts of the country had fallen behind and we would do something about them. I am not going to talk about the maritimes as they have many able representatives to speak on their behalf, but I am going to say something about what is going on in my own province of Manitoba. There was the south Saskatchewan dam, promised for years and years by the Liberals, but it took a Conservative government to bring it into being. The Columbia river project would be under way if it were not for one provincial government that cannot make up its mind.
What about Manitoba? I see the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill) smiling. For a long time I felt he was the spokesman for Manitoba, and it was a sorry day indeed when this government came to power. I expected as a good Manitoban with great ability, that the Prime Minister would instantly recognize this man and place the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in the seat immediately beside him. This, Mr. Speaker, was the man picked to be prime minister once before. It is a sorry thing that a man of such great ability was put in such position as house leader and Secretary of State. I feel I must speak up for him because he is much more deserving of a higher position than that which he received.
In Manitoba we have the Winnipeg floodway. We have an associated system of dams and water conservation projects, and the biggest thing to come to Manitoba has been the Whiteshell nuclear research establishment in my own constituency of Springfield. What does that mean to us? I first entered politics as a young student in 1953 because of the fact that 90 per cent of the young people were leaving Springfield on account of lack of opportunities. What is Springfield today? It has been described as the jewel in the crown of Manitoba, and one of the greatest projects in it has been this Whiteshell nuclear research establishment. It was brought there under the

The Address-Mr. Slogan national development policy of the Conservative government to stimulate those parts of the country that were falling behind. I hope all hon. members of the house will have the opportunity of coming to see it.
There are some 600 men working there at present, and in a few months there will be some 500 people living in the new townsite there. Well over $20 million has been spent, and I think eventually the expenditure will probably be well over $200 million. What does it mean? It is not just the construction jobs that it provides for the people from Manitoba and elsewhere, but it is the jobs it is going to provide for the brilliant young men in universities in the research program for the peaceful uses of atomic energy. These young people who at one time had to leave the province and the country to seek opportunities elsewhere can now find opportunities on their own doorstep.
During the last election campaign the Liberal party in Manitoba had a television or telethon program, or something like that, where you 'phoned in questions. One of my constituents 'phoned in a question and received a letter from the Liberal party of Manitoba in which they said:
The Whiteshell nuclear project has not been nor ever will be a campaign issue. The Liberal party has in the past, and will continue to support the establishment of all such similar projects for the province of Manitoba.
I was interested to listen to the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Konantz) when she said that she and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) are going to do such great things for Manitoba. Well, my hon. friends, where were they when the present Prime Minister, who claims to have such a broad national outlook, was trying to take this project away from Manitoba and put it into his own riding? The Minister of Veterans Affairs sat mute in the Manitoba legislature. Where is he now? The only thing he has done for the west is fire one of the most capable men on the veterans' pension commission. If that is the greatest contribution he is going to make to western Canada he may as well pack his bags and move to Ottawa, because surely this is not why the people of Manitoba elected him.
The Liberals paid great lip service to this nuclear project. Let us look at the headlines of just a little while ago. Here is a headline of the Beausejour Beaver of February 3, 1960, "Pearson for moving nuclear centre". Then we see this headline, "Liberals increase pressure against research centre". This is the kind of pressure that was brought to bear by the Liberal party in trying to take this project away from Manitoba and put it in the Prime Minister's own riding. There were marches

on Ottawa. Do hon. members remember the march of the women from Elliot Lake? They said there were 500 of them. I counted them; there were only 150. They did everything they could, and the present Prime Minister was the leader in the fight to take this project out of Manitoba and put it in his own riding. Is that a viewpoint for a national leader to take? Is this the national viewpoint of the Liberal party? If it is, it is little wonder that they received the verdict they did from western Canada. That is exactly the verdict they will continue to receive.
I talked about the north. We had that vision of the north. Do hon. members know what the present Prime Minister, that great leader with national vision, said? He said, when we brought in our roads to resources program, "You are building roads from igloo to igloo." Does not that harp back to the days when we were trying to build Canada and bind it together with the C.P.R.? They said in those days that we were building railways from tepee to tepee. The philosophy of the Liberal party has not changed. The philosophy of the Conservative party has not changed, because we adopt that same basic attitude toward our nation's problems and our nation building that we had in those days. It is little wonder that Harry Boulette-who was a Liberal candidate in the provincial election, I believe, in Manitoba in 1958 or 1959-came out in this election and supported me. He said that the policies of the former Liberal government had bankrupted the north country. He is known as the king of the north. He said that the policies of the Conservative government had breathed new life into the north country. It is no wonder the Liberals received such a small percentage of the votes in the north country, because when their own party supporters and party candidates desert them, they must indeed be bankrupt of ideas. Harry Boulette was not the only one. There was the candidate in Brandon-Souris who deserted the party because of their nuclear stand. He led an anti-nuclear demonstration in Winnipeg during the campaign. Therefore one does not wonder at the verdict given by the people of western Canada to this government.
I think it is about time that instead of fragmentation policies they sought to unite this country. I for one will be waiting eagerly for the ministers on the other side of the house to get up one by one and declare what are these nation building policies they are going to bring forth. I would like to see them brought forth, because we will certainly support them if they are good for Canada.
I must compliment the backbenchers of this parliament, because they are most certainly better behaved than were the backbenchers of the last parliament. We are not

going to behave in any way like the Liberals behaved last December 19. Do hon. members remember that day-

A friend of mine, after witnessing that incident, said, "You know, the House of Commons was once a gentlemen's club where most of its members spent their time hunting and shooting. In the few minutes I have at my disposal, Mr. Speaker, I should like to acquaint the house with my constituency. It stretches from Winnipeg to the Ontario boundary; it goes 300 miles north; it covers some 30,000 square miles of territory, and there are 50,000 people in it who are representative of all nationalities and all creeds. It is a Canada in miniature. We have suburban areas and we have vast areas where you can go 100 miles without seeing a person. We have Indians, Metis, Ukrainians, Poles, Germans and people of all nationalities who came in the great immigration under the Liberal government-and I give them credit for this-not as immigrants but more as colonists, who settled, worked hard and built Canada. The sons and daughters of these people are, like myself, taking their place in the forefront in professions, business and all walks of life. As I said before, I regret that this government has not seen fit to recognize the people who represent one quarter of this country's population.
I hope the present Prime Minister will correct this and correct it soon because I think these people are very deserving. In saying this, I take nothing away from our other people. I spent some time in Quebec. The first school I went to was a French school that did not teach English. I have a great deal of respect for all nationalities and I have great respect for Canada. My only plea is that we look to Canada first, that we do not fragment our nation, that we do not fragment our policies. I think the government can count on the support of every hon. member in this house if they bring in policies which have as their basic aim the building of a great, united Canada for the betterment of future generations. If those policies are brought forth, then the government need not worry about being defeated in this house. But so long as they fragment our nation, so long as they adopt this narrow, partisan point of view which does not see the forest for the trees, then Canada will indeed be in a sorry state, and if it is it will not be long

Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with those who spoke before me to congratulate you on your appointment as Speaker of the house.
I should also like to commend the Deputy Speaker on his own appointment and the mover (Miss Jewett) and seconder (Mr. Choquette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne who are the pride of the new and youthful Liberal team.
As the member for Gaspe, I am glad that the throne speech deals with questions which are of special concern to underdeveloped areas. It is the first time that a throne speech holds such promise for underdeveloped and labour surplus areas like Gaspe.
My riding which is a tourist attraction has a population of 65,300, 29,800 of whom have the right to vote.
In the first few months of 1963, there were 6,000 unemployed; three quarters of them received unemployment benefits and the others social security benefits.
Mr. Speaker, some people are alarmed when the unemployment level reaches 6, 7 or 8 per cent of the labour force in Canada. In my constituency, it goes over 50 per cent in wintertime and winter lasts six months down our way.
The federal legislation which was enacted in these last few years to relieve unemployment did not do so much for the underdeveloped areas of Quebec and the maritimes, but especially for the Gaspe peninsula.
During the past seven years, I was secretary treasurer of the town of Chandler and there are facts I know from personal experience which I should like to put on record mainly concerning the winter works program.
That legislation is more favourable to western municipalities and those of central Canada than to communities located in the province of Quebec and in the maritimes.
There are two seasons in Gaspe, summer and winter. This year, the winter works program covered the period from October 15 to May 31 regardless of whether the works were being carried out in Halifax, Chandler, Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver.
My colleague in the House of Commons, the member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deach-man) arrived in Ottawa around May 10 for the opening of the session and he told me that, before he left the Pacific coast, tulips

The Address-Mr. Cyr in Vancouver were a thing of the past and that summer flowers were in bloom.
On May 10, this same day, I had lunch with the students of the classical college of Gaspe seminary, and this same morning, my car became stuck during a snow storm at Murdoch ville.
The municipalities in my constituency can hardly benefit from the winter works program, because there is too much snow and the weather is too cold.
The Department of Labour will have to set up a committee to review the law and regulations governing the winter works program. When the time comes to pick out the members for this study, we will have to choose people from underdeveloped areas.
Mr. Speaker, the enacting of other legislation to help the areas suffering from chronic unemployment was not favourable to Gaspe peninsula. The point is about order in council No. PC-1961/326 amending the Income Tax Act in order to help industries in a surplus labour area.
The authorities of the town of Chandler and of 12 municipalities in the area submitted a brief in 1961 asking that our area be declared a surplus labour area.
On April 24, 1961, the deputy minister of labour replied as follows:
As you know, a survey was conducted last spring to see whether the village of Chandler could be recognized as an area of surplus labour for the purposes of the special capital cost allowance program. It has been ascertained that the area was not meeting the conditions required to be classified as such under the program.
To be recognized as a surplus labour area, (1) an area must have been classified by the Department of Labour in the surplus labour area category for at least 50 per cent of the summer months from 1953 to 1960 and (2) employment must have decreased during the same period. Our survey of the situation discloses that the village of Chandler has been classified in that category for less than 50 per cent of the necessary period and that employment in Chandler has increased during the same period. As you can see, Chandler meets neither of the two conditions.
Since the designation is based on the trend of employment and of unemployment during the period 1953-60 and since, according to the reports, your area does not meet the conditions, I hope you will understand that it would not be of much use to make a new survey.
Yours truly,
George V. Haythorne.
Mr. Speaker, during the fifties I was placement officer of the unemployment insurance office in Chandler, and I can assure you that the statistics related to the unemployed were in accordance with the applications filed at the office, but they did not give a real picture of the conditions prevailing in that area.
The Gaspe population was aware of the fact that there were no jobs available in the forest industry, in the building industry or elsewhere. So they felt that it was useless to report to a local office for employment since jobs were not available.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock? (Text):
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
